units.la: ASsertionum siue Thesewn Posnaniensium de Ecclesia auctor Arturus, societatis, quā Iesuiticam blaphemè vocant, sectator tres libros emisit, quibus illarum Analysin & Refutationem oppugnat: ea duntaxat reponens argumenta quæ à Turriano & aliis eiusmodi proposita, iam ita fuerūt antè refutata, ut Christiano Lectori negotium nunc amplius facesse re non debeant. Veruntamē quum Nobilissimi viri P.M. Domini Antonij Sadeelis opera in vnum volumen redigerentur, repertæ sunt Animaduersiones ipsius manu scriptæ ad marginem librorum Arturi (qui sero tamen ad ipsum peruenerat) quibus illi libri strictim refelluntur. Decreuerat autem præstantissimus ille vir integrum de Ecclesia tractatum scribere, in quo omnes in hoc argumento Aduersariorum obiectiones collectas, & quasi in vnum fasciculum congestas, simul semelque refutaret: quod inutilis foret laboris, istorum Repetitas cauillationes quotidie nouis Responsionibus refellere. Sed quum tam præclarū opus non construxerit: noluimus tamen Lectorem Christianum carere illis tanti viri tam egregiis animaduersionibus siue notulis, quas alioquin, si dignos hoc labore istos Arturi libros iudicasset, vberiore stylo & copiosiore oratione illustrasset.
units.tr: The author Arturus, a follower of the society which they blasphemously call Jesuit, has published three books attacking the analysis and refutation of the Assertions of Posen concerning the Church. He repeats only those arguments which Turrianus and others of that sort have already put forward, and which have been refuted so thoroughly that they should no longer give the Christian reader any trouble. However, when the works of the most noble man, the late Master Antoine de Sadeel, were being collected into one volume, his own handwritten notes were found in the margins of Arturus's books (which reached him only late). In these notes those books are briefly refuted. That outstanding man had intended to write a complete treatise on the Church, in which he would gather together all the objections of the opponents on this subject and refute them at once in one bundle. This would have been a waste of effort, since it would mean refuting their repeated cavils every day with new answers. But since he did not complete so excellent a work, we have nonetheless not wished the Christian reader to go without those notes of so great a man, which are most striking. Had he judged these books of Arturus worthy of such labour, he would have illustrated them in a fuller style and a more copious discourse.

units.la: Breuem igitur Arturi declamationum (sunt enim tres istius libri, pueriles potius declamentiunculæ, quàm legitimi tractatus nūcupandi) Redargutionem, quæ sit tanquam Appendix ad superiorem Analysin & refutationem Assertionum Posnaniensium, hac methodo nūc proponimus: vt quæcunque in illis traduntur, ad tria capita reuocentur. Horum primum est de Digressionibus: alterum, de Calumniis & Conuitiis: tertium de sophisticis argumentis. In quorum Refutatione ita versabimur, vt ad duo priora capita, vel nihil, vel admodum pauca respondeamus. Illa enim nudè tanquam digito monstrata, satis per se refelluntur. Tertium vero caput diligentius excutietur, & argumenta omnia ab isto proposita,quantum fatis erit refel-lentur: hac etiam ratione ( ne Le-ctor repetitionibus oneretur ) vt notemus eorum Refutationem vt plurimum iam aduersus Turrianu institutam,a quo iste illa sua plera-que interpolauit. Istorum autem Monachorum scribendi & diffe-rendi ratio, ita fuit in Præfatione tractatus de verbo Dei a D. Sadee-le expressa, vt eius tanquam lucu-lentissimum exemplum Arturus nunc proferat.Ex quibus omnibus Arturus blasphemę sodalitatis fiue Monachus fiue Clericus, non tan-quam leo ex vnguibus: sed vt afi-nus calfitrofus ex auribus, vel tan-quam canis ex allatratu facilè de-prehendetur.
units.tr: Therefore we now offer, in this method, a brief refutation of Arturus's declamations (for these three books are rather childish little declamations than legitimate treatises, and deserve no other name), which is meant as an appendix to the earlier analysis and refutation of the Assertions of Posen. Everything they contain will be reduced to three heads. The first is on digressions; the second, on calumnies and insults; the third, on sophistical arguments. In refuting these we shall proceed so that we answer little or nothing to the first two heads, since those are set out bare, as if pointed at with a finger, and are refuted well enough by themselves. The third head will be examined more carefully, and all the arguments this man puts forward will be refuted as far as is sufficient. In doing so, so that the reader is not burdened with repetitions, we shall note that their refutation has for the most part already been directed against Turrianus, from whom this man has borrowed most of his material. The manner of writing and arguing of these monks was set out in the preface to Sadeel's treatise on the Word of God, and Arturus now brings it forward as a most striking example of it. From all this it will easily be recognised that Arturus, whether monk or cleric of that blasphemous brotherhood, is revealed not as a lion by his claws, but as a kicking donkey by his ears, or as a dog by its barking.

units.la: Cæterum, tres iste libros suos ita inscripsit : De Christi in terris Ecclesia. Quanam & penes quos existat, Libri tres. Et simul Apologia Assertionum eiusdem infcri-ptioptionis contra falsas Antonij Sadeelis crimi-nationes. Quorum potius hæc debet esse ἐπιγεφὴ, vt ea legitimè propo-nat, quæ in illis tractantur. Repetitio argumentorum quæ à Turriano, Duræo & Bellarminio desumpta fuerunt: vna cum Con-uitiis & variis Digressionibus pro defensione Pseudocatholicæ Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ Romanæ. Itaque nisi esset istorum impuden-tia detegenda, atque minus exerci-tatis consulendum, qui putant istos Monachos, aliquid magni profer-re, aut aliquid noui edere, quum eorum libros sesquipedales vident: nulla amplius opus foret responsione alia, quàm ea quæ aduersus illos & similes monachos de hoc Ecclesiæ argumento extant in tra-ctatibus accuratissimè conscriptis ab eximiis Dei seruis D.Beza, D. Sa-deele, D. VVittakero, & aliis eiusmodi præstantissimis viris. Etsi e-nim isti blasphemæ nouæ societatis sectatores omnem iampridem pudorem exuerunt, pene tamen incredibile est, isti Arturo in mentem venire potuisse, vt in hac declamatoria scribendi ratione sibi tantopere aduersus illum placeat, qui e contrario nihil nisi apposite, solide, enucleate & pie scribere consueuerat, scilicet quasi rhetorculi monachi quasi simiæ saltantis tripudio possit eludi veritas, in hoc præsertim argumento quod in genere didascalico ἀποδεικτικῶς tractandu esse cöftat. Certe si ἐχεμυθίαν ipse tibi indixisses, Arture, melius tibi cauisses, aut si saltem tuis promissis stetisses, quum in tui libri præfatione ita aiebas: Conuitiis cum quopiam certare mihi neque honorificum cen seo, neque decorum, sed facere non possum, inquiebas, quin argumenta Sadeelis confutem. Hoc, inquam, si tantum præstitisses: ea quæ verbosissimis istis tribus libris persequutus es, vt tuam bilem ἀνεφηλον expleres, paucu-lis paginis esses complexus: quem-admodum ex sequentibus manife-stum fiet.
units.tr: Moreover, he has given these three books of his the following title: On the Church of Christ on Earth: Which It Is and Where It Exists, Three Books. Together with an Apology for the Assertions of the same title, against the false slanders of Antoine de Sadeel. A better title, one that would properly set out what is treated in them, would be this: A repetition of the arguments taken from Turrianus, Duraeus and Bellarmine, together with insults and various digressions in defence of the pseudo-Catholic Papist Church of Rome. Accordingly, were it not necessary to expose the impudence of these men, and to advise those less practised who think these monks are producing something great or publishing something new when they see their books of a foot and a half in length, there would be no further need for any answer other than the one already given against these monks and their like on this subject of the Church, in the treatises most carefully written by the eminent servants of God, Master Beza, Master Sadeel, Master Whitaker and other most distinguished men of that kind. For although the followers of this blasphemous new society cast off all shame long ago, it is almost incredible that it could have occurred to Arturus to take such pleasure in this declamatory manner of writing, against a man who, on the contrary, was accustomed to write nothing but aptly, solidly, clearly and piously. As if truth could be mocked by the dancing of a monkish little rhetorician, like the capering of an ape, especially in a subject which is plainly to be treated in a didactic genre demonstratively [ἀποδεικτικῶς]. Certainly, Arturus, if you had imposed silence [ἐχεμυθίαν] on yourself, you would have looked to your own interests better; or if at least you had kept your promises, when in the preface of your book you said: I think it neither honourable nor fitting to contend with insults against anyone, but I cannot help refuting Sadeel's arguments. I say, if you had done only this, you would have condensed into a few pages what you have pursued through these very wordy three books, in order to vent your bile [ἀνεφηλον]; as will become manifest from what follows.

units.la: {a}ARTURO de se suisque sodalibus imprimis sollicito valde dolet quod Sadeel Iesuitas, quorum sit tamen, scilicet, nomen sanctissimum & innocentissimum vitae genus, ad Iscariotem relegarit. Principia vero suae illius tam sanctae societatis arcessit, primum ex his Apostoli verbis, 1. Cor. 1. 9. Vocati estis in societatem Filij Dei Iesu Christi Domini nostri:& ex hoc loco.1. Ioan. 1.3. vt societas nostra sit cum Patre & Filio eius Iesu Christo. At quaenam haec impudetia est, quod totius a codito mundo Ecclesiae verae commune est, & a quo Ecclesia Christiana ex omnibus gentibus collecta, Catholicae, cognomentu accepit, iltos praevaricantes hypocritas audere sibi vt propriu vendicare? Necsane temere factum est vt qui prius discipuli Iesu Christi appellabantur, maluerint Christiani a Christo, quam Iesuitae a Iesu appellari. Est enim nomen Iesu gloriosius, augustius, diuinius denique, quam vt vlli vel Angeli iure possint ab ipso denominari, vnico omniu Seruatore. Christiani vero a Chrià Christo denominati, quid ab illo consequatur, ostendunt, qui prior secundùm carnem vnctus est, vt summus & vnicus ille nolter Rex, Propheta & Sacerdos: vt ipsius fiant coheredes. Et boni illi sodales à Spiritu sancto, scilicet, hoc sunt peculiariter consequuti vt Iesuitæ etiàm ipsi, idest, noui Seruatores mundi, dicî & palàm nuncupari merentur.
units.tr: Arturus, being especially anxious about himself and his fellow members, grieves greatly that Sadeel has consigned the Jesuits (whose name, to be sure, is most holy, and whose way of life is most innocent) to Judas Iscariot. He draws the origins of that so-called holy society first from this saying of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 1:9, You are called into the fellowship of the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, and then from this passage, 1 John 1:3, that our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. But what sort of shamelessness is it that these hypocritical law-breakers dare to claim for themselves as their own the name that belongs in common to the true Church of the whole world since its creation, and from which the Christian Church gathered from all nations has received the name Catholic? And it is no accident that those who were formerly called disciples of Jesus Christ preferred to be called Christians from Christ rather than Jesuits from Jesus. For the name of Jesus is more glorious, more majestic, and in short more divine than that any angels, even, could rightly be named from it, since he is the only Saviour of all. The Christians, however, named from Christ the Anointed, show what follows from it: he was anointed first according to the flesh, so that he might be that supreme and only King, Prophet and Priest of ours, and so that they might become his co-heirs. And those good fellows, by the Holy Spirit, have, to be sure, attained this especially: that they deserve to be called, and openly named, Jesuits, that is, new saviours of the world.

units.la: Huic autem firmo nimirum fundamento aliud etiam non minùs futile superstruit Arturus, illa videlicet, quæ de Iessæis ab Epiphanio traduntur: quo nomine ait scribens aduersus Nazaræos, prius vocatos fuisse Christianos à Iesse Dauidis illo celeberrimo patre. Sed nullo testimonio ac ne coniectura quidem vlla probabili nititur illud Epiphanij, Iessæos istos proculdubio malè discernentis ab iis quos cæteri scriptores ac præsertim Philo, & ipsemet Panarij fui lib. 1. Essenos appellauit. Hos autem sanè facilè patiemur istius, quam illi iactant societatis auctores censeri, vt qui, eodem Epiphanio teste, Spiritum sanctum non admiserint: imò etiam ignorarint, ex quibus Iessitæ vel Iessæi vel Essni non Iesuitæ erunt appellandi. Quid interea verò noster Arturus? Ex quibus, inquit, colligitur, societate Iesuiam extitisse Apostolorum temporibus, non nouam, vt calumniatur Sadeel. O miserâ igitur Christianam Ecclesiam, in qua tot seculis latuit vna & quidem prima Samaritanorum secta eodem Epiphanio teste, donec tandem bono illo patre Ignatio, num è cœlis an potiùs ex inferis, ad illam orbi Christiano patefaciendam excitaretur:quam saltè nobis liceat vt ex frudtibus ar- borem,id est, ex his ipsis Arturi verbis digno- fcere. Nufqnam fixi fumus, inquit, eijs domicilia firma habeamus, nusquam stamus, nusquam fede- mus : tot nos calamitosa prouincia, agrota Resp. b. nec cogitantes accersunt, totfolicitant cura, tot vr- gent negotia. Ipsa tamen non Monachorum est, sed Clericorum fociotas, vt ex sacrata Tridentina Sy- nodo apparet, &c.Enimuero magnus est hic sal- tus ab Apoftolorû temporibus ad Tridentinû recens Conciliabulum, cui ne omnes quidem etiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ Principes fubfcri- pserunt. Illa vero,quum legis, Christiane le- ctor, annon ipsum audire Christum tibi vide- ris totidem istis verbis hypocritas istos eandé operâ peruerse nauantes atque olim Scribæ & Pharisæi reprehendentem, væ vobis, inquit, Scribæ & Pharisæi qui circumitis mare & aridam vt faciatis vnum Proselytum, & quum fueritfactus, facitis eum filium gehenna duplo magis quam vos. Quónam enim isti non excurrerunt & adhuc excurrunt, secum omne superstitionis genus, discordias cædes, bella, omnis denique diuini & humani iuris horrendam violationem, at- que adeo miseris cæteris monachis exitium fe- cum trahentes ?quod heu! Gallia nunc ac ni- mium infelix istis in sinû receptis serpentibus præ cæteris Regnis, experitur. Hinc altura illa appellationis Monachorum euitatio ne ipsi sese mutuo expellere,sicuti de præda digladia- ri grassatores solent, monachi videantur, in quorum nidos,isti nouitij irrepunt: vt vere de istis mihi dicere liceat quod de serpentibus aic PliPlinius : ipsos videlicet minutis aliis voratis serpentibus euadere dracones. Hæc enim sunt firma illa quæ ipsi vocat, domicilia: noui scilicet Apostoli, (sed neque a Christo designati, neque Apostolorum successores) quorum nihilominus in Ecclesia Catholica gubernatio non aliis quàm totius orbis terrarum finibus circumscribatur. Nusquam enim, inquit Arcturus, stamus, nusquam sedemus. Ergo nusquam requiem inuenniut isti, vt qui sunt ex illorum impurissimorum Spirituum genere, quos ait Lucas II. 16. nusquam cessare donec septem alios spiritus peiores quàm sit ipse inueniat, vt domum ex qua fuerat eiectus regressus, nouissima reddat prioribus deteriora. Sed quid eos iuuat istud, siue Monachorum, siue Clericorum nomen? Nam quod ad Monachos attinet, Spiritus Sanctus aut Lateranensi Concilio non præfuit, aut in Tridentino seipsum abnegauit, quod vtrunque istis facilè largimur. Sic enim illud Concilium cap. 13. Ne nimia, inquit, religionum diuersitas grauem in Ecclesia Dei confusionem inducat, FIRMITER PROHIBEMVS (ea videlicet firmitate, qua omnes Conciliorum Canones apud Pontifices Romanos stabiles censentur) nequis de catero nouam religionem (idest, Monasticum ordinem) inueniat: sed quicunque voluerit ad religionem conuerti, vna de approbatis assumat. De Clericis autem in Concilio Constantinopolitano primo sic cauetur. Monachi post annum tricesimum possunt fieri Clerici. Ergo boni viri facti eitis Clerici per saltum, vt Romæ Domini d Rota loquuntur, aut neque monachi neque Clerici vnquam fuistis. Habent enim Clerici suam parœciam eligendi sunt ab Episcopo, & ipsi vicissim Episcopum eligere cum testimonio & consensu plebis debent, Canone nullus distinct.24. Can.de Clericis: Can.illud quoque Can.de aliena Ecclesia Canon.siquis. Can.primatus Can.extraneo.distinct.71. At tu Domine, Iesu Christe, quando tandem apparebis è cœlis existorum luporum Pseudomonachorum & Pseudoclericorum faucibus oüiculas tuas asserturus?
units.tr: To this, surely, firm foundation Arturus adds another, no less flimsy one, namely what is handed down about the Iessaeans by Epiphanius. He says, writing against the Nazarenes, that the Christians were formerly called by this name from Jesse, that most famous father of David. But that statement of Epiphanius rests on no testimony, nor even on any probable conjecture, since it plainly misidentifies those Iessaeans with the people whom other writers, and especially Philo, and Epiphanius himself in his Panarion book 1, called Essenes. We will readily allow, however, that these men are not the founders of that society which they boast of, since, by the same Epiphanius's testimony, they did not admit the Holy Spirit; indeed, they did not even know from whom the Iessitae or Iessaeans or Essenes, and not the Jesuits, were to be named. What, meanwhile, does our Arturus say? From these things, he says, it is gathered that the Jesuit society existed in the times of the Apostles, and is not new, as Sadeel slanders. O miserable Christian Church, in which for so many centuries one sect lay hidden, and indeed the first sect of the Samaritans, by Epiphanius's testimony, until at last, under that good father Ignatius, it was roused, whether from heaven or rather from hell, to be revealed to the Christian world! Let us be allowed, at least, to recognise the tree from its fruits, that is, from these very words of Arturus. We have never settled, he says, so as to have firm dwellings; we never stand still, never sit down; so many calamitous provinces, so many sick people, not even thinking of us, summon us; so much care worries us, so many tasks press upon us. Yet the society is not of monks but of clerics, as appears from the sacred Synod of Trent, and so on. Indeed, what a great leap this is, from the times of the Apostles to the recent Trent conciliabulum, which not even all the princes of the Roman Church signed! And when you read those words, Christian reader, do you not seem to hear Christ himself rebuking these hypocrites, who labour at the same perverse work, and once did so with the Scribes and Pharisees, in those very words? Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he has been made, you make him a child of hell twice as much as yourselves. For where did those men not run, and where do they still run, bringing with them every kind of superstition, discords, slaughters, wars, and in short the dreadful violation of all divine and human law, dragging down with them the other wretched monks to ruin? This, alas, unhappy France now experiences more than other kingdoms, since she has received these serpents into her bosom. Hence that lofty avoidance of the title of monks, so that they themselves may appear to be monks, which they drive out of each other as robbers usually fight over plunder; into whose nests these novices creep. So I may truly say of these men what Pliny says of serpents: that they escape by devouring other small serpents, and so become dragons. For these are the firm dwellings that he speaks of: new apostles, to be sure, neither designated by Christ nor successors of the Apostles, whose government of the Catholic Church nevertheless is bounded by no limits other than those of the whole earth. For we never, says Arturus, stand, we never sit. Therefore these men find rest nowhere, since they belong to the kind of most impure spirits, of whom Luke says (11:26) that they never cease until they find seven other spirits worse than themselves, and returning to the house from which they had been cast out, make the last state worse than the first. But what does that name, either of monks or of clerics, help them? As for monks, the Holy Spirit either did not preside over the Lateran Council, or in Trent he denied himself; both of which we readily grant to them. For the Council says in chapter 13: Lest too great a diversity of religious orders induce grave confusion in the Church of God, WE FIRMLY FORBID (with that firmness, of course, by which all the canons of the Councils are reckoned stable among the Roman Pontiffs) that anyone henceforth invent a new religion (that is, a monastic order), but whoever wishes to be converted to a religion, let him take up one of the approved ones. Concerning clerics, the First Council of Constantinople lays down as follows: Monks after the thirtieth year can become clerics. Therefore, good men, you have become clerics by a leap, as they say in the Roman Rota, or you were never monks nor clerics. For clerics have their own parish, and they are to be chosen by the bishop, and they in turn must choose the bishop with the testimony and consent of the people, as in the canon nullus, distinction 24, the canon de Clericis, the canon illud quoque, the canon de aliena Ecclesia, the canon siquis, the canon primatus, and the canon extraneo, distinction 71. But you, Lord Jesus Christ, when at last will you appear from heaven to rescue your little sheep from the jaws of these false monks and false clerics, these savage wolves?

units.la: Arturus fidem implicitam vrgens eam nobis proponit, quæ in dæmonas etiam cadir, multò videlicet quàm isti sint sacræ historiæ callentiores, quum istorum plerique nihil minùs quàm sacras literas curent. Sed hæc quæstio toties refutata, alium tractatum requirit.
units.tr: Arturus, pressing implicit faith upon us, proposes that faith to us, which falls even upon demons, far more evidently than those men are more skilled in sacred history, since most of them care for the sacred letters least of all. But this question, so often refuted, requires another treatment.

units.la: Idem Arturus probaturus Pontificios lectionem Scripturæ in linguis vernaculis minimè prohibere, testatur ipsos è contrario desisse operam vt Sacra biblia omnibus prope linguis ederentur. Nos verò Deo gratias agimus quòd tandem istos ad palinodiam adegerit. Quàm enim furiosè permultis annis istorum, quas vocant, fadultates Theologicæ prohibuerunt sacros libros in eas linguas verti, quibus possent à quibusuis legi, immò, quàm multos eo nomine vt hæreticos damnarint, qui hos libros ita versos apud se haberent, quis ignorat, præter istos, quosnihil pudet? Sed ipsi interea egregiè caucrunt, scilicet, nequod inde detrimentum acciperet Ecclesia ipsorum RomaRomana, ea fide tum sacris libris, tum Veterum & Recentiorum quoque doctorum scriptis plerisque ea fide editis, vt nullum sit falsitatis genus cuius non possint manifestissime coargui.
units.tr: Arturus, wishing to prove that the Papists do not in the least forbid the reading of Scripture in the vernacular tongues, testifies that they, on the contrary, have ceased to work for the Holy Bible being published in almost all tongues. We, however, give thanks to God that he has at last driven them to this recantation. For who does not know how furiously, for very many years, the so-called Theological Faculties of those men forbade the holy books to be turned into those tongues in which anyone could read them, and how many they condemned as heretics on that account, for keeping such translated books among themselves, except these men, who are not ashamed of anything? But meanwhile they have taken very careful precautions, namely that their own Roman Church should suffer no harm from this, by publishing, with such good faith, both the sacred books and the writings of the ancient and recent teachers, most of them so faithfully edited, that no kind of falsehood is there which they cannot most clearly be convicted of.

units.la: Excurrit Arturus praeterea in locos aduersus Pseudoecclesiam Romanam à nostris prolatos super Iustificatione per fidem. lib. 2. cap. 11. sicuti de Charitate lib. 3. cap. 34. & de variis aliis dogmatibus cap. 35. quali vero in hoc de Ecclesia articulo haec omnia tractari oportuerit. Seorsum autem ista sunt à nostris iampridem copiosissime & verissime suis quaeque locis explicata.
units.tr: Arturus also goes on at length against the passages our people have brought forward against the false Roman Church concerning justification by faith (book 2, chapter 11), as well as on charity (book 3, chapter 34) and various other doctrines (chapter 35). But these matters should not have been treated in this article on the Church at all. Our writers long ago explained each of them fully and accurately in their proper places.

units.la: Agit praeterea Arturus de Sacramentis inter quę matrimonium & Confessionem & cetera eiusmodi recenset lib. 2. cap. 13. & 14. & lib. 3. cap. 41. quaecunque ipsi libuit nostris affingens, & eò vsque pro suo Catholico Romano zelo proiectus vt panem quem in sacra Domini Coena, prout Dominus constituit consecratum distribuimus, ausus sit sexcentis sacrilegiis contaminatum, & aptiorem Daemonibus quàm hominibus escam appellare. At nos ab iistis tuis mendacissimis & impurissimis mendaciis, ad ipsius Christi tribunal provocamus.
units.tr: Arturus also deals with the sacraments. In book 2, chapters 13 and 14, and book 3, chapter 41, he lists marriage, confession and similar things, attaching to our people whatever he pleased. His zeal for the Roman Catholic cause has carried him so far that he has dared to call the bread we distribute in the Lord's Supper, consecrated as the Lord instituted it, contaminated by six hundred sacrileges and a food fitter for demons than for men. But we summon you, and your most lying and impure lies, before the tribunal of Christ himself.

units.la: Quid amplius? Arturum ne istud quidem laudare pudet, quòd Pontifices pedemferico telum & cruce munitum solerent deosculandum porrigere, cuius rei, inquit, origo non inuenitur. Quare igitur subinde afflagitas vt dicamus quo anno defecerit Ecclesia Rom. & quis Pō. tifex errores primus introduxerit? Certe in nul-lis sacris libris nec veteribus patribus istud de osculatione crepidæ inuenitur. Sed veram eius descriptionem apud Ioannem inuenies, vbi describit purpuratam illam meretricem septem illis montibus, & inde Principibus excæcatis dominantem (& quoniam hoc quoque diuina prouidentia constituit) in Adriani Imperatoris Mausoleo, quam in arcem fallissimo Sancti Angeli nomine cognominata transformauit, sede profecto Principis Mortis vicario digna collocatam, suo tempore, quod meretur, exitium senseram. Quod autem hic a nobis postulat Arturus, vt doceamus, quo anno & quo sedente Pontifice cœperit Ecclesia Romana & eius Episcopi a Christiana fide deficere, partim est a nostris, quantum id quidem ex historiis colligi potest, & ex diuini verbi cum doctrina illius sedis, qua & Hieronymus ipse Babylonem, & Petrarcha templum hære-ticum appellat, collatione manifeste apparet. Nos autem ab hac scabie toties refricata vn-gues vltro abstinemus. In quo etiam albo re-censemus illa diuerticula quæ idem Arturus, millies refutata subinde, relicta quæstio-ne, digrediens, excurrit capite 13. & 14. & 19. lib. 3. & pag. 358. de libris Machabæorum. De Scripturæ obscuritate & auctoritate. De Monachis, cap. 32. De Romanorum Episcoporum laudibus, lib. 3. cap. 23. De Reprobis, quasi ad Ecclesiam Catholicam quæ Christi corpus est, pertinentibus, lib. 1. cap. 13. & 14. & 17. 18. 19. 20. 28. 30. & pag. 129. 130. & 131. Et lib. 3. cap. 34. Fabulas
units.tr: What more is there? Arturus is not even ashamed to praise this: that the Popes used to offer their foot, armed with a spear and a cross, to be kissed. He says the origin of this custom cannot be found. Why then do you keep demanding that we say in what year the Roman Church fell away, and which Pope first introduced these errors? Certainly this custom of kissing the sandal is found in no sacred books nor in the ancient Fathers. You will find its true description in John, where he describes that purple harlot ruling over those seven hills and, through her blinded princes (as divine providence also ordained), set up in the Mausoleum of the Emperor Hadrian. Under the most deceitful name of St Angelo she made it into a citadel, a seat truly worthy of the vicar of the Prince of Death. In its own time it felt the ruin it deserved. As for what Arturus demands of us here, that we show in what year, and under which reigning Pope, the Roman Church and its bishops began to fall away from the Christian faith, this is partly set out by our writers, as far as it can be gathered from the histories, and it is plainly evident from comparing the doctrine of that see with the word of God, which is why Jerome himself calls Babylon, and Petrarch calls it a heretical temple. We, however, willingly refrain from scratching this sore, which has been rubbed so often. In this same list I enumerate the digressions which Arturus, digressing and leaving the question aside, runs into again and again, though they have been refuted a thousand times: in book 3, chapters 13, 14 and 19, and page 358, on the books of the Maccabees; on the obscurity and authority of Scripture; on the monks, chapter 32; on the praises of the Roman bishops, book 3, chapter 23; on the reprobate, as if they belonged to the Catholic Church, which is the body of Christ, book 1, chapters 13, 14, 17, 18, 19, 20, 28 and 30, and pages 129, 130 and 131, and book 3, chapter 34.

units.la: Digressio septima, octava, nona, decima, undecima. bulas denique de Protestatium, quos appellat, Ecclesia & doctrina lib.3.cap.13 14. & 35.37.38. 39. contemptu, quàm repetitis refutationibus digniores.
units.tr: Digression seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven. Finally, the fables about the contempt shown to what he calls the Protestants' Church and doctrine, book 3, chapters 13, 14, 35, 37, 38 and 39, which deserve refutation more often than they have received it.

units.la: DE CONVITIIS ET CALVMNIIS quibus vsus est Arturus.
units.tr: Of the Insults and Calumnies with which Arturus Abounds.

units.la: Arturus tres illos suos libros ita Conuitiis & Calumniis instituit, vt vix aliud sit in illis quod possis ἀ ἀλυέιν: quibus replevit pag.1. 2. 6 7. 11 12. 15 16 18 28 29.30.31. 32 34 47 48.127. 128.132.140 141.142 143 144.145.147. & 210.170. Et lib.3 c. 8 10. 14 30 35. & 38. & pag. 269.270. 332.334 &c. quas paginas & capita notamus: vt lectores istius κακοήθειαν, & tractandi rationem monachis consuetam, agnoscant.
units.tr: Arturus has so filled those three books of his with insults and calumnies that there is hardly anything in them one could call ἀ ἀλυέιν [not to be borne]. He has stuffed them into pages 1, 2, 6, 7, 11, 12, 15, 16, 18, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34, 47, 48, 127, 128, 132, 140, 141, 142, 143, 144, 145, 147, and 210, 170. Also in book 3, chapters 8, 10, 14, 30, 35, and 38, and pages 269, 270, 332, 334, and so on. I note these pages and chapters so that readers may recognise this κακοήθειαν [malice] and the method of handling opponents that is customary for monks.

units.la: Ad Conuitia verò & Calumnias eiusmodi quod attinet, quarum plenas hamaxas in vivos & mortuos omnes illos omni exceptione maiores Theologos diuinitus hoc nostro seculo excitaros passim euomuit, tum veteres illas innumeras calumnias sine vllo pudore reponens, tum infinitas alias commiscens, vt impuriffimi canis latratus ne tantillum quidem moramur, de hoc potius solliciti vt per bonam & malam famam ad palmam nobis propositam perpetuo cursu contendamus.
units.tr: As for the insults and calumnies of this kind, of which he everywhere pours out full quivers against all the living and the dead, those theologians who in our age have been raised up by God, men greater than any exception, I do not even pause over the barking of this most filthy dog, reproducing as he does those old countless calumnies without any shame and mixing in endless others. Rather, let us be concerned only with this: that, running our perpetual course through good report and bad, we strive for the prize set before us.

units.la: CAPVT I. REFVTATIO ARGVMENTORVM quae Arturus proposuit ad impugnandam Analysin & Refutationem Assertionum Posnaniensium de Ecclesia.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. REFUTATION OF THE ARGUMENTS that Arturus put forward to attack the Analysis and Refutation of the Posnanian Assertions concerning the Church.

units.la: MVltafunt hic dicenda de Ecclesiæ dignitate & præstantia(inquit assertor Arturus blasphemæ sodalitatis sectator) eiusque præconia apte in illis assertionibus fuerunt à me adhibita: contra quàm Sadeel existimet, qui dicit illud esse ςπερ- γον. Nam quæstio de Ecclesia compendiaria est ad omnes differentiones tollendas. Omnes enim hæretici in controversia de Ecclesia succumbunt. Et Sadeel ipse refugit de Ecclesia tractationem.
units.tr: "Many things must be said here about the dignity and excellence of the Church," says the assertor Arturus, a follower of that blasphemous fraternity, "and I have applied its praises fittingly in those assertions. Sadeel, however, thinks otherwise and says that this is superfluous [περίεργον]. For the question concerning the Church is a short cut to removing all differences. All heretics succumb in the controversy about the Church. And Sadeel himself shrinks from treating of the Church."

units.la: Est magni proculdubio momenti tractatio de Christi Ecclesia de qua dicuntur hæc in Scriptura, quæ monachorum præconia longè superant. Ephes. 1. Eum (nempe Christum) constituit caput ipsi Ecclesiæ: quæ est corpus ipsius. Eph 2. & Col. 3. reconciliavit utrumque in uno corpore, Vocavit in unum corpus. Ephe. 5. Ecclesia est ipsa Christi, non habet maculam aut rugam. Membra sumus corporis eius. Gal. 4. Sublimis Hierusalem libera est, quæ est mater omnium nostrum. 1. Tim. 3. Ecclesia est domus Dei, columna & firmamentum veritatis. 1. Cor. 12. Per unum spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus. Rom. 12. & 1. Cor. 10. Unum corpus multi sumus: & pler/ aque eiusmodi quæ in Scriptura & apud veteres Ecclesiasticos doctores extant. Quæ quidem omnia ad illam Ecclesiam pertinent, quam nos credecredere in fidei fimbolo profitemur: quæ est Communio sanctorum, cui Remissio peccatorum & vita æterna per Christum tribuitur: éstque ipsa Ecclesia catholica ex solis electis, à Christo sanctificatis, redemptis & vitâ æternâ donandis constituta. Ephse.5. Illa vero, vt ad aliquem cœtum visibilem etiam pertinere vere dicantur, prius demonstrandum est, illum in terris visibilem cœtum, fidem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ ex electis constitutæ, constanter retinere: idque ex sacra Scriptura docendum, quia per hanc, ab Apostolorum prædicatione, Spiritus sanctus Ecclesiam in terris, quæ pars sit illius Catholicæ, colligit & ædificat. Rom. 1. & 10. Ioan.20.1.Cor.4. 6.Luc.1.2. Pet.1 & 3.1. Ioan.2. &c.Nō oportet igitur Ecclesiæ nomine abuti, æquiuocè multis cœtibus perperam attribuito: quò credamus, ad illos omnes qui illud sibi arrogant, ea referri quæ de vera Christi Ecclesia dicuntur: nisi perspectum habeamus, eos Christi doctrinam genuinam seruare: vt exarticulis fidei dignoscatur, penes quos extet Ecclesia, & ex illis Ecclesia constituatur.
units.tr: Without doubt, the treatment of Christ's Church is a matter of great importance, and what Scripture says of it far surpasses the praises of the monks. Eph. 1: "He (namely Christ) appointed him head over the Church, which is his body." Eph. 2 and Col. 3: "He reconciled both in one body"; "He called us into one body." Eph. 5: "The Church is his own, having no spot or wrinkle; we are members of his body." Gal. 4: "The Jerusalem above is free, which is the mother of us all." 1 Tim. 3: "The Church is the house of God, the pillar and ground of the truth." 1 Cor. 12: "By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body." Rom. 12 and 1 Cor. 10: "We, being many, are one body." And there are many similar passages in Scripture and in the early ecclesiastical teachers. All of these certainly pertain to that Church which we profess in the creed to believe: the communion of saints, to which forgiveness of sins and eternal life are granted through Christ, and which is the catholic Church itself, constituted solely of the elect, sanctified, redeemed by Christ and destined for eternal life. Eph. 5. But before these things can truly be said to pertain to some visible assembly, it must first be shown that a visible assembly on earth steadfastly retains the faith of the catholic Church, constituted of the elect; and this must be taught from holy Scripture, because through it, from the preaching of the Apostles, the Holy Spirit gathers and builds up the Church on earth, which is part of that catholic Church. Rom. 1 and 10; John 20; 1 Cor. 4; 6; Luke 1; 2 Pet. 1 and 3; 1 John 2, etc. It is therefore not right to abuse the name of the Church, or to attribute it equivocally and wrongly to many assemblies, so that we believe that everything said of the true Church of Christ refers to all those who claim it for themselves, unless we have clearly ascertained that they keep the genuine doctrine of Christ. By the articles of faith we must discern where the Church is, and from them the Church must be constituted.

units.la: Pontificij verò Romanenses de Ecclesia aduersus nos contendentes duplicem perpetuò errorem admittunt. Prior est: quòd de Ecclesia Romana perinde disserant, ac si illam veram esse Christi Ecclesiam, sponsam, columnam, & firmamentum veritatis, planissimè ex Dei verbo demonstrassent: itaque nobis illam proponunt, vt si verè iam probassent illam ipsam Ecclesiam Catholicam ipsam ad quam referre oporteat elogia & promissiones omnes quę de vera Christi Ecclesia in sacra Scriptura & apud veteres pios doctores exrant. Atqui nos negamus Romanā Ecclesiam pontificiam esse veram Christi Ecclesiam: imò illam æqui-nocè Ecclesiam dici, & nullo modo Catholicæ Ecclesiæ nomen illi conuenire, probamus. Alter error est: quòd Ecclesiam nolint ex doctrina diiudicari, & ex fidei Articulis dignoscì: sed contrà, fidei articulos, non ferendā audaciā, ex illo Ecclesiæ nomine metiri volunt: ita vt currus, quod aiunt, boues trahat. Non igitur mirum videri debet, quare Pontificij doctores dicant: quæstionem de Ecclesia compendiariā esse ad nos refellendos. Nam quum docemus eorum dogmata sacræ Scripturæ, ac proinde doctrinæ & Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ & verè Catholicæ repugnare: statim respondent, id fieri non posse, quum Ecclesia Catholica & Apostolica quæ est Romana Ecclesia, errare non possit. Hic nos efflagitamus vt ex Scriptura sacra aperte doceant rem tanti momenti: nempe vt credamus Ecclesiam Romanam esse illam Ecclesiā Catholicā & Apostolicam ad quam promissiones de salute sint referendæ, ita vt extra eam nulla sit nobis salus. Tunc illi pro sacra scriptura, libros quorundam monachorum hoc asserentium proferunt. Et Ecclesiam Romanam esse veram Christi sponsam vociferantur, quia pontifici omnes vno ore constanter illud volunt, illud affirmant, ac proinde quia ipsis ita lubet, hoc firmissimè credendum esse contendunt: quæ sanè nō modò impudens, sed puerilis etiam est ratio oratio. Ergo vt Pontificiis detrahatur larua: quoties aduersus illos de Ecclesia instituitur disputatio: semper prius proponenda est vera & essentialis Ecclesiæ definitio, ex qua, non ex solo nomine, Ecclesia Christi statuatur: Hinc demonstrandum est, cuinam coetui, illa definitio vere conueniat. Ideo sunt Articuli fidei qui in symbolo Articulum de Ecclesia præcedunt ex sacra Scriptura demonstrandi. Ex quibus elucescet: illam demum esse veram in terris Christi Ecclesiam quæ docet & proponit sacram doctrinam in verbo Dei comprehensam. Hac ratione dilucidè, certò & verè Christianè, constituetur: An Romana Ecclesia, quæ nunc est Pontificia: an vero Ecclesiæ Reformatæ sint Ecclesia Catholica Apostolica: hoc est, vera Christi Ecclesia.
units.tr: The Roman Papists, however, in contending against us about the Church, maintain a twofold and perpetual error. The first is that they discourse about the Roman Church as though they had clearly demonstrated from God's Word that it is the true Church of Christ, his bride, the pillar and ground of the truth; and so they put it before us as if they had already truly proved that this very Church is the catholic Church to which all the praises and promises that Scripture and the godly early teachers give of the true Church of Christ must be referred. Yet we deny that the Papal Roman Church is the true Church of Christ, and indeed we prove that it is called so only equivocally and that the name of the catholic Church in no way belongs to it. The second error is that they do not want the Church to be judged by doctrine and recognised by the articles of faith; on the contrary, they want to measure the articles of faith by that name of the Church, with an unbearable audacity, so that, as they say, the cart draws the oxen. It should therefore not seem surprising that the Papist teachers say that the question concerning the Church is a short cut to refuting us. For when we show that their dogmas contradict holy Scripture and consequently the doctrine and the Apostolic and truly catholic Church, they immediately reply that this cannot be the case, since the catholic and apostolic Church, which is the Roman Church, cannot err. Here we demand that they teach openly from holy Scripture a matter of such great importance: namely, that we must believe the Roman Church to be that catholic and apostolic Church to which the promises of salvation are to be referred, so that outside it there is no salvation for us. Then they bring forward, in place of holy Scripture, the books of certain monks who assert this. And they shout that the Roman Church is the true bride of Christ, because all the Pontiff's followers with one voice constantly wish it, affirm it, and therefore insist that, because it pleases them, this must be firmly believed. Surely this is not only an impudent argument but even a childish one. Therefore, to strip the mask from the Papists, whenever a dispute about the Church is undertaken against them, the true and essential definition of the Church must always be set out first, and from it the Church of Christ must be established, not from the name alone. Hence it must be shown to which assembly that definition truly applies. For this reason the articles of faith that precede the article on the Church in the creed are to be demonstrated from holy Scripture. From these it will become clear that the true Church of Christ on earth is the one that teaches and sets forth the sacred doctrine contained in the Word of God. In this way it will be established clearly, certainly and truly as Christians: whether the Roman Church, which is now Papal, or the Reformed Churches, are the catholic apostolic Church, that is, the true Church of Christ.

units.la: Hæc autem omnia fusius explicata fuerunt à Doctoribus reformatæ Ecclesiæ: tum etiam fusè in Analysi superiore: in tract. de verbo Dei scripto. Et aduersus Turrianum & Monachos Burdegalenses & in tract. de legitima pastorum vocatione: quæ satis indicant Sadeelem non refugisse de Ecclesia quæstionem, vt hic Arturus inepte dictitat, non minus quàm absurdè paulo post sic ait. Obiicit Sadeel, Si vestra dogmata sunt Scripturæ consentanea, docete. Hoc, inquit Arturus, ostendo, quum doceo penes nos Ecclesiam existere. At hoc illud est, egregie Assertor, quod est demonstrandum, & illud ipsum in disquisitione positum est: quomodo igitur id poterit ad illud postulatum confirmandum adhiberi?
units.tr: All these things have been explained more fully by the teachers of the Reformed Church, and also at length in the earlier Analysis, in the treatise on the written Word of God, against Turrianus and the Burdigalian monks, and in the treatise on the lawful calling of ministers. These sufficiently show that Sadeel did not shrink from the question of the Church, as Arturus foolishly keeps saying, and no less absurdly says shortly afterwards: "Sadeel objects: If your dogmas are consistent with Scripture, teach them." "This I am showing," says Arturus, "when I teach that the Church exists among us." But this is precisely what is to be demonstrated, and it is exactly the point under dispute. How, then, can it be used to confirm that very postulate?

units.la: Obiicit Sadeel Tabulas nunquam exhibetis. Respondeo (inquit Arturus) ex Constantinop. synodo, vnam, sanctam Catholicam & Apostolicam notas Ecclesiæ quas in septem claritatis causa partitus sum. In hoc conuenimus, quod virique Ecclesiam ex verbo Dei potissimum cognoscendam iudicemus: saltem hoc tempore propter pertinacia m hæreticorum, qui nihil recipiunt quod in diuinis libris non extet. Illud differimus, quod tu Symbola minus apta, nos autem aptissima statuamus. De notis Ecclesiæ suo loco. Sed cur iste Asertor quouis tempore, & omnino non admittit Ecclesiam ex verbo Dei dignoscendam esse? Nam symbola & decreta Veterum synodorum, vel omnino nituntur verbo Dei, vel plane sunt reiicienda. Ita etiam refelluntur quæ ab Arturo subiiciuntur. Traditiones Apostolicas vocare humana decreta nefarium est.
units.tr: "Sadeel objects: You never produce your tables. I reply," says Arturus, "from the Council of Constantinople, the notes of the Church: one, holy, catholic and apostolic, which I have divided into seven for the sake of clarity. We agree in this, that both of us judge that the Church must be known chiefly from the Word of God, at least at this time, because of the obstinacy of heretics, who accept nothing that is not found in the divine books. We differ in this: you set up creeds that are less suitable, whereas we set up the most suitable." The notes of the Church will be discussed in their proper place. But why does this assertor not admit, at any time and not at all, that the Church is to be recognised from the Word of God? For the creeds and decrees of the ancient councils either rest wholly on the Word of God or must be plainly rejected. In this way too, what Arturus adds is refuted. "To call Apostolic traditions human decrees is wicked."

units.la: Nam traditiones Apostolicæ extant in verbo Dei scripto: reliquæ sunt vt plurimum commentitiæ & à quibusdam monachis fabricatæ: præsertim illæ quæ verbo Dei repugnant, quæ nō possunt esse Apostolicæ. At, inquit Arturus, omnium gentium consensio est naturæ lex inquit Cicero: Ergo omnium Christianorum conspiratio lex quoque Christi existimari debet. Hæc & similes obiectiones, in tract. de verbo Dei scripto, & aduer. Turrianum, fuerunt refutatæ. Hoc tamen adiiciendum. Theologica pronuntiata esse ex sacra Scriptura depromenda. Christus enim est vnicus in sua Ecclesia Legislator, non natura, aut gentium ius, aut hominum placita. Conspiratio autem Christiaftianorum nulla est:nisi verus consensus,quum se verbo Dei vnanimiter subiiciunt.
units.tr: For Apostolic traditions are found in the written Word of God; the rest are for the most part invented and fabricated by certain monks, especially those that contradict the Word of God, since these cannot be Apostolic. "But," says Arturus, "the consent of all nations is the law of nature, says Cicero. Therefore the agreement of all Christians ought also to be regarded as the law of Christ." These and similar objections were refuted in the treatise on the written Word of God and against Turrianus. Yet this must be added: theological pronouncements must be drawn from holy Scripture. For Christ alone is the Legislator in his Church, not nature, nor the law of nations, nor the decrees of men. Moreover, there is no agreement of Christians, except a true consensus, when they submit themselves unanimously to the Word of God.

units.la: Ecclesia non potest esse sine miraculis, inquit Arturus. Hoc enuntiatum a Turriano saepius, & iam ab illo Arturo, tum hic,tum lib.3. cap. 28.repositum,fallax & captiosum esse:in tract. de legitima vocatione & adu. Turr. multis in locis, & in Indice artic. 14. fusè explicatum fuit.
units.tr: The Church cannot exist without miracles, says Arturus. Turrianus has often repeated this statement, and now Arturus repeats it here and in book 3, chapter 28. It is false and deceptive. I explained this fully in the treatise on lawful calling and against Turrianus, in many places, and in the index under article 14.

units.la: Pontifex,inquit Arturus,dicitur caput Ecclesiae:sed Ministeriale ex Chrysost.hom.55.in Matt. & Concil.Chalcedon. De capite Ecclesiae Ministeriali,vt istorum subterfugia tollantur,& de testimoniis corruptis ab isto repetitis. aduer. Turrian.fusè. In Indice articul.30. ad repet.eiusdem Sophismata in loco Scrip. 1. artic. 19. 20.27.28 29. Et in loco.2.articul.49.Et loco.6. articul.8.Et loco 11.articul.9. Et aduersus eiusdem Sophismata priora loco script. 2. Et ibi ad reper.Sophism.articul.58.vbi indicatum est locum illum ex Chrysostomo ab Arturo ex obiectionibus Turriani descriptum,falsò citari, aliàque verba pro Chrysostomi verbis substitui. Illis etiam in locis aduersus istos demonstratum est: In Ecclesia Apostolica non fuisse caput vnum Ministeriale totius Ecclesiae. Hoc enim & Scripturae & Ministerij naturae repugnat, exiplis etiam Veteribus conciliis. Imò etiam in Concilio Lugdun. sic loquebantur Episcopi : Omnes membra sumus, sub vno nostro capite Christo coadunati. Et hi scripturae loci illud commentitium caput Ecclesiae Pontificium conterunt, Ephes. 1.
units.tr: The Pope, says Arturus, is called the head of the Church, but in a ministerial sense, citing Chrysostom, homily 55 on Matthew, and the Council of Chalcedon. I have dealt fully with the ministerial headship of the Church, and with the corrupted testimonies that he repeats, in my reply to Turrianus, so that their evasions may be removed. See the index, article 30, on the repeated sophisms in the first passage of Scripture, articles 19, 20, 27, 28 and 29; in the second passage, article 49; in the sixth passage, article 8; and in the eleventh passage, article 9. Against his earlier sophisms, see the second passage of Scripture, and there the index on the repeated sophisms, article 58, where it was shown that Arturus cites that passage from Chrysostom, taken from Turrianus's objections, falsely, and that other words have been substituted for Chrysostom's. In those same places it was shown against them that the Apostolic Church had no single ministerial head of the whole Church. This contradicts both the nature of Scripture and the nature of the ministry, as the ancient councils also show. Indeed, at the Council of Lyons the bishops spoke in this way: We are all members, gathered together under one head, Christ. And these passages of Scripture overthrow that invented Papal "head of the Church": Ephesians 1.

units.la: Eum constituit caput super omnia ipsi Ecclesiæ quæ est corpus ipsius, Ephes. 4. Adolescamus in eum qui est caput, nempe Christum, Ephes. 5 vir est caput vxoris vt Christus est caput Ecclesiæ, Col. 1. & 2. Christus est caput corporis Ecclesiæ, &c.
units.tr: He appointed him head over all things to the Church, which is his body, Ephesians 4. Let us grow up into him who is the head, namely Christ, Ephesians 5. The husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the Church, Colossians 1 and 2. Christ is the head of the body, the Church, and so on.

units.la: Capite sexto libri primi, & cap. 7. & 10 & 22. & 27. lib 3. Arturus asserit: Protestantes cum Donatistis & Apostolicis habere commercium ex Augustino, &c. Nos esse Nouatianos: item quod negemus ἐξομολόγησιν. Ar quia Pœnitentiam Confessionem auricularem reiicimus, non idcirco reiicimus veram peccatorum confessionem, quæ verbo Dei nititur. Nihil autem nobis commune esse cum Donatistis & Nouatianis facile quidem refellimus. Quòd ad Apostolicos attinet, eorum dogmata quæ Bernardus recenset, non sunt damnenda.
units.tr: In chapter 6 of book 1, and chapters 7, 10, 22 and 27 of book 3, Arturus asserts that the Protestants have fellowship with the Donatists and the Apostolics, according to Augustine, and so on, and that we are Novatians, and also that we deny confession [ἐξομολόγησιν]. But because we reject auricular confession and penance, we do not thereby reject the true confession of sins, which rests on the Word of God. We can easily refute the claim that we have anything in common with the Donatists and the Novatians. As for the Apostolics, the doctrines which Bernard lists are not to be condemned.

units.la: Cæterum, quum tam vehemens, tamque diuturna fuerit Augustini cum Donatistis contentio, eáque permultis libris copiosè ab ipso Augustino explicata: & hodie Pontifcij solent ex Augustini pharetra tela quædam deprimere aduersus nostras Ecclesias, quoties de veris Ecclesiæ notis, adeóque de vera Ecclesia instituitur disputatio, aliquid de hac re nobis est dicendum.
units.tr: Moreover, since the dispute between Augustine and the Donatists was so vehement and so long-lasting, and since Augustine explained it at great length in very many books, and since today the Papists are accustomed to draw certain weapons from Augustine's quiver against our Churches whenever the true marks of the Church, and so the true Church itself, are debated, I must say something about this matter.

units.la: Liber de vnitate Ecclesiæ ab Augustino conscriptus videtur summam continere eorum omnium quæ aliis in libris sæpe aduersus Donatistas inculcauit: quorum hæc est summa, vt etiam aduersus Turrianum & In Tract. de legit. vocatione pastorum, fuit explicatum.
units.tr: The book on the unity of the Church, written by Augustine, seems to contain a summary of all the things he often impressed in other books against the Donatists. The gist of it is this, as was explained also against Turrianus, and in the treatise on the lawful calling of ministers.

units.la: Donatiftæ, commoti corruptiffimi orbis Chriftiani moribus, exiftimabat Ecclefiam in maxima parte orbis terrarum defecifle, quum peccati contagione alij alios corrupiffent: itaque feccefferunt, vt ab illa contagione eximerent: affirmarunt apud fe tantum Ecclefiam remanfiffe: fplendorem Ecclefiæ ad folos mores reftringentes.
units.tr: The Donatists, moved by the very corrupt morals of the Christian world, thought that the Church had fallen away in the greater part of the earth, since people had corrupted one another by the contagion of sin. So they withdrew, so as to be freed from that contagion. They maintained that the Church had remained only among themselves, restricting the splendour of the Church to morals alone.

units.la: Contrà : Auguftinus quia Donatiftæ fibi fumebant apud fe folos effe Ecclefiam, obiicit promiffiones de Ecclefia Chriftiana, cenfêtque Ecclefiam illis Africæ partibus aut aliis locis vbi erant Donatiftæ minimè aftrictam effe:fed Ecclefiam Chriftianam, hoc eft veram Ecclefiam nullis locis circumfcribi, nulli gentì ab Apoftolorum temporibus aftringi: fed per vniuerfum terrarum orbem effe diffufam : ac proinde Donatiftas ab Ecclefiæ Chriftianæ communione recedentes, effe extra Ecclefiam. Iam, obfecro, quis iure Donatiftas nobis poteft obiicere, aut quid commune habent argumenta noftra cum Donatiftarum argumentis? Nos enim doctrinam ipfam ex verbi Dei præfcripto reformandam affirmus: neque propter mores folos Ecclefiam Romanam Pontificiam reiicimus. Negat Auguftinus fequi Ecclefiam defecifle propter numerum improborum. Et nos hoc etiam agnofcimus. Negabat Auguftinus Ecclefiam effe reftringendam ad Donatiftas qui erant in Africa: & nos eodem argumento vtimur aduerfus Romanum Pontificem, quum docemus promiffiones quæ extant in verbo Dei erga veram Christi Ecclesiam, minime restringendas esse ad illam sedem Pontificiam, aut ad Ecclesiam Romanam. Statuebat Augustinus manente doctrina manere Ecclesiam. Nos etiam hoc vrgemus. Augustinus denique Donatistas ex S. Scriptura refellebat. Hoc hodie in his controuersiis prœstandum esse contendimus. Docet Augustinus zizania esse semper in Ecclesiis visibilibus: & nos hoc agnoscimus: qui propter solos mores corruptos secessionē faciendam non esse ab illa Ecclesia quæ veram doctrinam profitetur, docemus. Cæterùm Donatistarum argumenta nullius erant momenti. Nam hærebant in hoc paralogismo. Catholicorum mores sunt corruptissimi: Ergo nulli sunt ampliùs fideles. Item: Ergo desecit & apostatauit Ecclesia. Error duplex ἀπὸ τὸ ἐπόμενον: Prior: quia non sequitur, Multi sunt vitiosi & scelerati: Ergo, Omnes. Posterior: quia Apostasia refertur ad doctrinam ipsam potiùs quàm ad mores. Iam Donatistæ subsistebant in moribus: cæteroquin amplectentes Catholicorum doctrinam. Perpetramergo ratiocinabantur. Impudenter etiam ita connectebant. Si Ecclesia vbique defecit: Ergo à nobis solis est instauranda, qui sumus aliis meliores. Hic non ratione modò, sed pudore etiam destituebantur. Nam ipsi (qui tamen erant hypocritæ, vitæ inquinatissimæ) prædicabant suam Ecclesiam perfectam vitæ integritate (vt hodie Anabaptistæ, monachi & Clerici pseudonymi) qualis nunquam fuit diffusa: quia sagena Apostolica collegit multa,& ex omni genere: & Ecclesia Apostolica semper est precata : Remitte nobis peccata nostra.Refutatio autem ab Augustino propositta, in multis quidem est solida, sed in aliis visa est imbecillior. Nam quum toties vrget promissiones de Diffundenda Ecclesia per totum orbem, non propterea tollebat obiectionem Donatistarum. Primùm:quia non promisit Dominus, Ecclesiam ita vbique diffundendam, vt semper maneat in eodem statu. Habet enim Ecclesia suos progressus: habet item suos defectus instar lunæ: cuius similitudinem veteres in hac quæstione crebro vsurpant. Et ille ipse Augustinus hanc doctrinam agnouit: quid ni enim agnoscceret? quum res ipsa loquatur, & id veteres historiæ luculentissimè confirmént? Exempla sint de Arianis,de Turcis, &c. Deinde non sequitur:Oportuit Ecclesiam diffundi:ergo nunquam in illis locis apostatabit.Nā manifesta fero ἐνςραση ex. 2. The. 2. Porrò illa diffusio Ecclesiæ nō fieri debuit simul & semel: sed progressu temporis. Nec etiam facta Diffusio debuit semper in eodem statu permanere. Quid ergo? Nempe quum de Ecclesia agitur, & demonstrandum est penes quos exstat: veniendum est ad ea quæ sunt ἀποστολικαὶ Ecclesiæ, & ipsam Ecclesiam constituunt: cuiusmodi est puritas doctrinæ & fidei veritas.Proponenda igitur sunt semper in hac quæstione hæc Theoremata.
units.tr: Against this, Augustine, because the Donatists claimed that they alone were the Church, set against them the promises about the Christian Church. He judged that the Church was by no means confined to the parts of Africa, or to other places, where the Donatists were, but that the Christian Church, that is, the true Church, is bounded by no places and tied to no nation since the times of the Apostles, but is spread through the whole world. Therefore the Donatists, who withdrew from the communion of the Christian Church, were outside the Church. Now, I ask you, who can rightly object this to us, or what do our arguments have in common with the arguments of the Donatists? For we affirm that the doctrine itself must be reformed according to the prescription of the Word of God, and we do not reject the Roman Papal Church on account of morals alone. Augustine denies that the Church has fallen away because of the number of the wicked, and we acknowledge this too. Augustine denied that the Church was to be confined to the Donatists who were in Africa, and we use the same argument against the Roman Pontiff, since we teach that the promises which stand in the Word of God concerning the true Church of Christ are by no means to be restricted to that Papal see, or to the Roman Church. Augustine maintained that while the doctrine remains, the Church remains. We also insist on this. Lastly, Augustine refuted the Donatists from Holy Scripture. We contend that this must be done today in these controversies. Augustine teaches that tares are always present in visible Churches, and we acknowledge this; we teach that because of corrupt morals alone one must not secede from that Church which professes the true doctrine. Moreover, the arguments of the Donatists were of no weight at all, for they rested on this paralogism: the morals of the Catholics are most corrupt; therefore none of them is any longer faithful; and again, therefore the Church has fallen away and apostatised. This is a double error from the consequent [ἀπὸ τὸ ἐπόμενον]. The first: because it does not follow that since many are vicious and wicked, therefore all are. The second: because apostasy relates to doctrine itself rather than to morals. The Donatists remained fixed on morals, while otherwise embracing the doctrine of the Catholics. Thus they reasoned perversely. They also joined the points shamelessly: if the Church has fallen away everywhere, then it must be restored by us alone, who are better than the others. Here they lacked not only reason but also shame. For they themselves (who were nevertheless hypocrites, of most polluted life) proclaimed their Church perfect in the integrity of its life, as the Anabaptists, the monks and the pseudo-clergy do today; yet such a Church was never widespread, since the Apostolic net gathered many fish, of every kind. And the Apostolic Church has always prayed: Forgive us our sins. The refutation set forth by Augustine is indeed sound in many respects, but in others it seems weaker. For although he insists so often on the promises that the Church would be spread through the whole world, he did not thereby remove the objection of the Donatists. First, because the Lord did not promise that the Church would be spread everywhere in such a way that it would always remain in the same state. The Church has its progress, and it also has its defections, like the moon; the ancients often used this comparison in this question. And Augustine himself acknowledged this doctrine. Why would he not acknowledge it, since the thing itself speaks, and the ancient histories confirm it most clearly? Examples are the Arians, the Turks, and so on. Next, it does not follow that because the Church ought to have spread, it will therefore never fall away in those places. For the working of error [ἐνέργεια] is plainly set out in 2 Thessalonians 2. Moreover, that spread of the Church ought not to have happened all at once; it was to come with the passing of time. Nor, once it had happened, ought the spread to have remained forever in the same state. What then? Namely, when we are dealing with the Church, and it must be shown where it exists, we must come to those things which are the Apostolic marks of the Church and constitute the Church itself, such as the purity of doctrine and the truth of faith. Therefore in this question these theorems must always be put forward.

units.la: 1. Si manet Doctrina Apostolica, manet etiam Ecclesia Apostolica. Nam vniras in doctrina, vt docet Tertullianus, Ecclesiæ vnitatem statuit.
units.tr: 1. If the Apostolic doctrine remains, the Apostolic Church also remains. For unity in doctrine, as Tertullian teaches, establishes the unity of the Church.

units.la: 2. Ecclesia quæ est corpus Christi, nūquam potest in terris deficere: quia Christus caput Ecclesiæ manet in æternum: Licet in terris non semper extet eadem facies Ecclesiæ: tamen sideri non potest quin semper sint aliqui pij, qui pure inuocent nomen Domini, & qui sint vera Christi membra.
units.tr: 2. The Church, which is the body of Christ, can never fail on earth, because Christ, the head of the Church, remains for ever. Although the same face of the Church may not always be visible on earth, it cannot be that there are not always some godly people who purely call upon the name of the Lord, and who are true members of Christ.

units.la: 3. Quandiu Ecclesia peregrinatur in terris erit malorum cum bonis commixtio.
units.tr: 3. As long as the Church sojourns on earth, there will be a mixing of the wicked with the good.

units.la: 4. Vbicunque sonabit sincera Euangelij prædicatio & erit legitimus Sacramentorum vsus, ibi erit Ecclesia, cui sese adiungere debent qui nomen Christianum vere profitentur.
units.tr: 4. Wherever the pure preaching of the Gospel sounds and the lawful use of the sacraments takes place, there is the Church, and those who truly profess the Christian name ought to join themselves to it.

units.la: 5. Morum depravatio non tollit Ecclesiam, modo sincera maneat Euangelij prædicatio. Nam fides est anima Ecclesiæ: & pluris esse debet sanctus vnus, quàm improborum centena millia. Intra hos cardines verti debuit disputatio contra Donatistas. Est autem impudentissimum nostras Ecclesias onerare Donatistarum vitiis & erroribus. Nos enim vrgemus (vt iam diximus, & sæpius dicendum est) depravationem doctrinæ Euangelicæ à Pontificis inuectam: non tantum hærentes in depravatis eorum moribus. Neque hic vel illic Ecclesiam alligamus: neque dicimus Ecclesiam plane defecisse: licet per aliquot secula eius facies, pontificiis tenebris obscurata sit. Hæc de disputatione Augustiniana aduersus Donatistas dicta sint, vt semel ad istorum obiectioctiones respondeamus, qui falsò & ἀγνοιαν τῶ ἐλέγχῳ obiiciunt nobis Donatistas. Nam quodnam est hoc argumentum? Augustinus Donatistas refellebat. Ergo Protestantes sunt Donatistæ, sicut illi damnandi. Nec enim ea docemus quæ Donatistæ: nec possunt Pontificij argumenta Augustini legitimè sibi vendicare.
units.tr: 5. The corruption of morals does not take away the Church, provided the pure preaching of the Gospel remains. For faith is the soul of the Church, and one holy man ought to be worth more than hundreds of thousands of wicked ones. Within these limits the dispute against the Donatists ought to have been conducted. It is, however, most shameless to burden our churches with the vices and errors of the Donatists. For we press (as we have already said, and must say often) the corruption of the Gospel doctrine introduced by the Pontiff, not merely clinging to their depraved morals. Nor do we confine the Church here or there, nor do we say that the Church has altogether failed, although for some centuries its face has been obscured by Papist darkness. Let these things be said about Augustine's dispute against the Donatists, so that we may once for all answer the objections of those who falsely and with ignorance of the refutation (ἀγνοιαν τῶ ἐλέγχῳ) charge us with being Donatists. For what kind of argument is this? Augustine refuted the Donatists. Therefore Protestants are Donatists, and deserve to be condemned as they were. For we do not teach the things the Donatists taught, nor can the Papists rightfully claim Augustine's arguments for themselves.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: REFVTATIO EORVM quæ Arturus proposuit aduersus 2. caput superioris Refutationis Assertionum Posnaniensium.
units.tr: Refutation of those things which Arturus has put forward against the second chapter of the earlier Refutation of the Posnanian Assertions.

units.la: Clesiam, inquit Arturus, in meis assertionibus non definiuisse nullus error fuit (ut Sadeel primum hunc errorem enumerans dicit) Nam ex thesium inscriptione clarum erat, me de Christi in terris Ecclesia disputationem instituere. Quis enim nescit Christi in terris Ecclesiam congregationem seu (ut Augustinus) conuocationem esse fidelium, vno cultu, vnáque fide inter se vinctorum? Nec tamen omnino definitionem praeteriui. Eo enim ipso quod Ecclesiæ partes percensui, eámque fideles omnes tam malos, quàm bonos, tam reprobos, quàm prædestinatos continere docui, hæreticos autem vt hostes repellere: Ecclesiam quodammodo definiui. Est enim Ecclesia sicut aggregatum per accidens cuius ea est conditio & natura, vt qui partes, ex quibus constat, distinxerit, ipsum quoque totum definiuisse censeatur. Hæc assertor Arturus.
units.tr: Arturus says: "It was no error in my assertions that I did not define the Church (as Sadeel says, listing this error first). For it was clear from the title of the theses that I was undertaking a discussion of the Church of Christ on earth. Who does not know that the Church of Christ on earth is the congregation, or (as Augustine puts it) the assembly, of the faithful, bound together by one worship and one faith? Nor, however, did I altogether pass over definition. For by the very fact that I enumerated the parts of the Church, and taught that it contains all the faithful, bad and good, reprobate and predestined, while repelling heretics as enemies, I have in a sense defined the Church. For the Church is like an aggregate by accident, whose condition and nature is such that whoever has distinguished the parts of which it consists is considered to have defined the whole as well." So the author Arturus.

units.la: Quanti sit autem momenti in quæstione de Christi in terris Ecclesia, ipsius Ecclesiæ definitio in superiori capite declaratum est. Hic vero Arturus quatuor Ecclesiæ definitiones profert, quarum nulla est quæ Ecclesiæ essentiam proponat. Nam prima quam vult ex libri inscriptione propositam fuisse definitionem, est inepta. Librorum enim ϐιβλιοθήκη non est definitio: Deinde illa inscriptio ipsam potius profert Conclusionem tractatus probandam: tantum abest ut sit vera definitio, quæ non demonstratur: sed demonstrat. Secunda definitio est potius descriptio. At hic quæritur Ecclesiæ ἐκκλησία definitio, quæ verum ipsius Genus, veramque differentiam eius specificam & essentialem constituat: ut nimirum ille Cœtus, siue congregatio ab aliis cœtibus vere secernatur. Itaque, ut sit plena definitio, oportet prius distinctione vt illa, quam in superiore capite propositumus: nempe Ecclesiam Catholicam siue vniuersalem eam esse quæ omnes fideles siue electos qui fuerunt, qui sunt, & qui futuri sunt, comprehendit, quæ sola est sponsa & corpus Christi. Ecclesiam vero in terris militantem & visibilem: esse partem illius Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, quatenus doctrinam retinet Christi, quam fideles & Electi seruant. Quum autem de hac potissimum Ecclesia in hac quæstione sit controuersia. fia, penes quos existat: sic illa est definienda. Ecclesia Christi in terris est cœtus fiue Congregatio hominum qui Christi doctrinam in ipsius verbo patefactam amplectuntur & retinent. Tertia definitio ab Arturo proposita, qua definit Ecclesiam ex partibus, quibus illam vult constare, non est admittenda. Nam Ecclesia, primùm non est dicenda constare ex Reprobis: quamuis multos esse Reprobos in cœtu & congregatione Ecclesiarum visibili non negemus.Neque etiam constat Ecclesia, (vt isti volunt, qui laicos, quos vocant,pro nihilo ducunt)ex pontifice Romano, Cardinalibus,Episcopis,sacrificulorum, & monachorum colluuie. Deinde homines ipsi ex quibus constat Ecclesia, rationem materiæ obtinent. At differentia fpecifica,non ex rei Materia,sed ex essentiali forma depromitur. Arturus igitur hic definitionem fine differetia essentiali profert, quæ non potest esse vera definitio. Absit autem vt ex Reprobis fiue damnandis Ecclesia Catholica, quæ est Christi corpus & sponsa, constituatur, quum illa ex communione sanctorum, hoc est solis Christi veris membris, fiue ex fidelibus, electis æternaque salute donnadis constet. Quarta Ecclesiæ definitio ab Arturo proposita, limilis est superiori: nisi quòd Ecclesia definire fe dicat, tàquam totum per accidens aggregatum:quod definiendi genus Turrianus totidem verbis proposuit, atque eo nomine definitio illa refutata fuit Adversus Turriani priora Sophismata loco 1.fcrip. & adipfius repet. loco 1. Art. 8. & 13. & 19. &c. in Indice. Sic porrò Arturus pag. 36. Sadeel in superiore Analysi origines Ecclesiæ minus Latinè status & appellationes vocat. Ipse tamen sui oblitus pag. 39. seipsum refellit, quum illud vocabulum in eadem significatione vsurpat, his verbis: varios status Ecclesiæ visum est operæpretium pernoscere, &c. Sed inepte iste dicit: Vnum habere varia principia, quatenus diuersas habet progressiones. Nam origo est vna, non plures: status vero & dispositiones possunt differre. Ideo hæc erant addita in super. Analysi. Vnius & eiusdem rei, vnum & idem principium esse constituendum: vnamque esse originem. At inquit Arturus: Vnus rei varia quasi principia Arist. in lib. de Anima genere constituere: quatenus diuersas habet in accremento progressiones. Respondeo Aristotelem ibi docere: totum partibus dissimilibus constans esse eiusmodi vt illarum partium vna possit esse prior tempore quàm altera in totius generatione. At nos hic dicimus Ecclesiam Christianam verè sic dictam, vnum habere principium, vnamque originem, variasque Ecclesiarum particularium dispositiones, non constituere diuersa Ecclesiæ Christianæ principia aut diuersas origines. Nec negamus Ecclesias particulares, ex quibus Ecclesia constituitur Catholica: alias aliis tempore priores esse. Nos igitur non de partium, sed de Totius principio verba facimus. Itaque locus Aristotelis imperitè fuit hic ab Arturo adhibitus. Sed operæpretiū est audire quæ syllogismū Arturus affingat. Nisi me omnia fallunt, inquit Arturus, pag. 38. hic est Sadeelis argumentationis sensus. Extra Ecclesiam Christi non est salus: Adam, Abel, &c. (quia in 5. errore enumerando Sadeel dixit cap. 2. Analysis superioris) non fuerunt in Ecclesia Christi, utpote pridem ante Christum. Ergo salutem adepti non sunt. Nihil Arturi nouus iste & ineptus Syllogismus habet quod referat argumentationem in superiori Analysi propositam, quum error Arturi hoc incommodo redarguebatur. Ipsum videlicet Ecclesiae Christianae initium, modo ab Abele, modo a die Pentecostes arcessentem inde ab illa Adamum excludere. Sic igitur potius fuit Arturo struenda argumentatio, ut legitime ea proferret quae de hac re in superiori Analysi proponebantur. Si verum est quod ait asserter Arturus: Ecclesiam nimirum, Christi Catholicam, vel die Pentecostes vel Abelis tempore initiu habuisse: Ergo hoc sequitur, duo esse unius Ecclesiae Catholicae initia: & ex ea Adamum ipsum excludi. Atqui utrumque absurdum est. Ergo initium Ecclesiae ab Arturo perperam fuit descriptum. Ex quibus intelligitur, Arturum non minus impudenter quam ineptè in his suis libris iactitasse velle se παιδευτὴν Sadeelis παιδείαν ipsiusque παιδευτικῷ esse: scilicet homo iste ἀπαίδευτος meliores & doctiores se erudiet: cuius ea est ἀπαιδευσία, ut nomen, ac multo magis rationem τῆς ἀπαιδείας vel ὀφηνίας ludibrio habeat. units.tr: How much weight the definition of the Church itself carries in the question of the Church of Christ on earth was explained in the previous chapter. Here, however, Arturus offers four definitions of the Church, and none of them sets out the essence of the Church. The first, which he says was put forward from the title of the book, is inept. For the title of a book [bibliotheke] is not a definition. Moreover, that title sets out the conclusion of the treatise that is to be proved; so far is it from being a true definition, which is not demonstrated but demonstrates. The second definition is rather a description. But what is sought here is a definition of the Church [ekklesia], which states its true genus and its true specific and essential difference, so that that assembly or congregation is truly distinguished from other assemblies. Therefore, to make a full definition, one must first add a distinction like the one we proposed in the previous chapter: namely, that the Catholic or universal Church is the one that comprises all the faithful, or elect, who have been, who are, and who will be, and which alone is the bride and body of Christ; while the Church militant and visible on earth is part of that Catholic Church, insofar as it retains the doctrine of Christ, which the faithful and elect keep. Since, however, the controversy in this question concerns chiefly this Church, and among whom it exists, it must be defined thus: the Church of Christ on earth is the assembly or congregation of men who embrace and hold the doctrine of Christ made known in his Word. The third definition proposed by Arturus, in which he defines the Church by the parts of which he wishes it to consist, is not to be admitted. For, first, the Church should not be said to consist of the reprobate, although we do not deny that there are many reprobate in the visible assembly and congregation of the churches. Nor does the Church consist (as those men think who count the laity, as they call them, as nothing) of the Roman pontiff, cardinals, bishops, and a rabble of sacrificers and monks. Next, the men of whom the Church consists take the place of matter, whereas a specific difference is drawn not from the matter of the thing but from its essential form. Arturus therefore here offers a definition without an essential difference, which cannot be a true definition. Far be it, moreover, that the Catholic Church, which is the body and bride of Christ, should be constituted out of the reprobate or the damned, since it consists of the communion of saints, that is, of Christ's true members alone, or of the faithful, the elect destined for eternal salvation. The fourth definition of the Church proposed by Arturus is similar to the previous one, except that he says he defines the Church as a whole aggregated by accident. This kind of definition Turrianus proposed in just these words, and on that account the definition was refuted in the reply to Turrianus's earlier sophisms, in the first place, and in its repetition, in the first place, article 8, 13, 19, and so on, in the index. Further, Arturus says on page 36: "Sadeel in the earlier Analysis calls the origins of the Church less Latinly its states and appellations." Yet he himself, forgetful of himself, refutes himself on page 39, when he uses that word in the same sense, in these words: "it has seemed worth while to learn the various states of the Church, etc." But he speaks foolishly: "a thing has various principles insofar as it has different progressions." For the origin is one, not many; the states and dispositions, however, may differ. That is why these things were added in the earlier Analysis: that for one and the same thing there must be one and the same principle, and one origin. But Arturus says: "Aristotle in his book On the Soul lays down that one thing has various, as it were, principles by genus, insofar as it has different progressions in growth." I reply that Aristotle there teaches that a whole made of dissimilar parts is of such a kind that one of those parts can be earlier in time than another in the generation of the whole. But we here say that the Christian Church, truly so called, has one principle and one origin, and that the various arrangements of the particular churches do not constitute different principles or different origins of the Christian Church. Nor do we deny that the particular churches, of which the Catholic Church is constituted, are earlier in time than one another. We therefore speak not of the principle of the parts but of the principle of the whole. Thus Aristotle's passage was here inexpertly employed by Arturus. But it is worth while to hear what syllogism Arturus invents. "Unless I am wholly mistaken," says Arturus, page 38, "this is the sense of Sadeel's argument: Outside the Church of Christ there is no salvation; Adam, Abel, etc. (because in enumerating the fifth error Sadeel said in chapter 2 of the earlier Analysis) were not in the Church of Christ, being long before Christ. Therefore they did not obtain salvation."
