That new and inept syllogism of Arturus has nothing that corresponds to the argument proposed in the earlier Analysis, by which Arturus's error was refuted on this point: namely, that by deriving the beginning of the Christian Church now from Abel, now from the day of Pentecost, he excludes Adam from it. The argument should therefore have been constructed by Arturus so that he might legitimately bring forward what was proposed about this matter in the earlier Analysis. If it is true, as the author Arturus says, that the Catholic Church of Christ had its beginning either on the day of Pentecost or in the time of Abel, then it follows that the one Catholic Church has two beginnings, and that Adam himself is excluded from it. But both are absurd. Therefore the beginning of the Church has been wrongly described by Arturus. From these things it is understood that Arturus, no less shamelessly than foolishly, boasted in these books that he wishes to be the teacher [paideutēn] of Sadeel's teaching [paideian] and of his instructive method [paideutikō], that is, that this uneducated man [apaideutos] would instruct his betters and more learned men, whose lack of education [apaideusia] is such that he makes a mockery both of the name and, much more, of the reason of his lack of learning [apaideias]. A wretched sophist, who also here disapproves of the scholastic method of refutation, by which fallacious arguments are marked with their names (though these alone are what these men's treatises are compounded of), so that they may more easily be detected by that method.

units.la: {y} Iac. 2. menta fallacia (quibus tamen solis istorum tractatus sunt confiati) vt ex illa methodo facilius detegantur. Hic certè Arturc, ἐξᾶλ᾽ ὁδέτι πῶ εἴπας ἐπος, ὡδ᾽ ἐτέλεσας: quum quid fit suo fe metiri pede non didiceris, prouinciam suscipiens temere & cum nimia φιλωτία, tuis humeris prorsus imparem.
units.tr: Here indeed, Arturus, "you have not yet uttered a word, and yet you have done it" [ἀλλ᾽ οὐδέ τι πω εἶπας ἔπος, ὧδ᾽ ἐτέλεσας], since you have not learned to measure yourself by your own foot, undertaking the task rashly and with excessive ambition [φιλοτιμία], wholly unequal to your shoulders. James 2.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: RTVRVS libro suo primo cap. 8. tertium caput Analysis superioris refellendum suscepit: his argumentis. Ad Ecclesiam Romanam, inquit, nulla possunt doctrinæ corruptelæ peruenire. At hoc illud est quod nostri salsissimum esse contendunt: idque ex doctrina de fidei Articulis in Dei verbo proposita demonstrant. Hinc enim, ad tollendam de Ecclesia penes quos existat, controuersiam, faciendum est inimum: non autem nudus Ecclesiæ titulus est proferendus: sicuti Iudæi olim Templum Domini, templum Domini magno oris hiatu lubinde prophetis obiiciebant eorum corruptelas redarguentibus. Quod si pontificia Ecclesia docet doctrinam salutarem in Dei verbo patefactam, cur hoc examen refugit, cur inde disputationem arcellere in hac controuersia, recusat? certè, si ostendamus illam lam non retinere hanc doctrinam,sed dogmata ei prorsus contraria docere:tum sole clarius apparebit illam falsò nomé Ecclesiæ vsurpare.
units.tr: Arturus, in his first book, chapter 8, undertook to refute the third chapter of the earlier Analysis, with these arguments: To the Roman Church, he says, no corruptions of doctrine can come. But this is the very thing our people hold to be most false, and they prove it from the doctrine of the articles of faith set out in God's Word. For to remove the controversy about where the Church is to be found, judgment must be made by this means, and the bare title of Church must not be put forward, just as the Jews of old kept throwing the Temple of the Lord in the faces of the prophets who rebuked their corruptions, shouting "the Temple of the Lord" with open mouths. But if the Papist Church teaches the saving doctrine revealed in God's Word, why does it shun this examination, and why does it refuse to bring the dispute into the open in this controversy? Certainly, if we show that it no longer retains this doctrine but teaches dogmas altogether contrary to it, then it will appear clearer than the sun that it falsely usurps the name of Church.

units.la: Reliqua quæ Arturus de fide implicita hic profert : & de versionibus sacræ Scripturæ, pertinent ad caput de Digressionibus, & de Calumniis. Nihil enim hic præterea protulit. Fides autem implicita qua vult Arturus Ecclesiæ dogmata niti, est tátum fides historica, quæ in ipsos dæmones cadit,vt docet Iacobus, atque toto-genere differt à vera fide quæ est πληροφορία,firmissimè promissiones Euangelij apprehendens quæ quidem ex auditione Doctrinæ Euangelicæ nascitur Rom. 10.& Christi membrorum tantum propria,quę Dei Verbo scripto, tanquam sui normæ, non autem Traditionibus humanis adhæret:vt copiosè in super.Analysi,aduersus Turrianum,& aduersus Monachos Burdegal.& in tractatu de verbo Dei demonstratum est.
units.tr: The rest of what Arturus here brings forward about implicit faith, and about the versions of Holy Scripture, belongs to the chapter on Digressions and the chapter on Calumnies. For he has offered nothing else here. The implicit faith on which Arturus wants the dogmas of the Church to rest is only historical faith, which falls even upon the demons, as James teaches, and differs in kind from true faith, which is full assurance [πληροφορία], firmly grasping the promises of the Gospel. Indeed, this faith is born from hearing the evangelical doctrine (Rom. 10), and it clings only to the proper members of Christ, and to the written Word of God as its rule, not to human traditions. This has been demonstrated at length in the preceding Analysis, against Turrianus, against the Monks of Bordeaux, and in the treatise on the Word of God.

units.la: Quod ad librorum sacrorum lectionem & versionem attinet: nequaquam nos admittimus corruptas & prophanas sacræ scripturæ versiones: nec earum interpretationem quibusuis committimus, vt Arturus falsò noltris impingit.Ex quibus colligimus Arturum nihil proposuisse:quominus hoc firmissimè constet:Ex sacra Scriptura controuersias de Ecclesia tollendas elles.
units.tr: As for the reading and the translation of the sacred books, we by no means admit corrupt and profane versions of Holy Scripture, nor do we entrust its interpretation to just anyone, as Arturus falsely charges against us. From this we gather that Arturus has proposed nothing that would make it more firmly established that controversies about the Church are to be settled from Holy Scripture.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: Chapter IV.

units.la: VARTVM caput superioris Analysis Arturus conatur refellere, multa de Reprobis proferens, vt probet eos ad Ecclesiam Catholicā, quę est corpus & spō sa Christi pertinere: idque prolixè persequitur à capite 10.ad 13.caput libri primi, & lib.2.c.2. Haec autem obiectio copiosè tractata fuit adversus Turrianum in Indice, Art.16.17.25. & adu. Repetita ipsius sophismata loco scripst. 1. art.8.Et loco 8.art.9 10.12 13. Et loco scripst.10. integro, in quibus omnia quæ de hac re Arturus, vestigiis Turriani tantùm insistēs, profert, refelluntur, quæ non sunt hic repetenda. Sophisticè autem Arturus subinde pro Responsione Exclamationem supponit. Sic pag. 60. Græcè & Latinè exclamat, ὦ συκοφάντα ... O fictum refugium! ὦ commentum! ὦ paradoxum! Quod si liberet ridiculum exclamatorem & declamatorem istum imitari, quibus verbis nos exciperemus istos, qui ut Ecclesiam Romanam esse Christi Ecclesiam, unumque ei caput visibile præficiendum probent, ad eam Reprobos pertinere contendunt! qui quasi Reproborum causam agat, blasphemè eos esse membra Christi asserunt! nimirum necogantur unum Christum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ caput vivificum agnoscere? Porrò in hac quæstione Arturus & reliqui sodales eius pervertia vtuntur μεταφορᾷ seu transpositione in vocabulis IN & DE. Nunquam enim negatum tum est: Reprobos esse in Ecclesiis visiblibus: hoc enim est manifestum. Sed negatur, Reprobos esse De Ecclesia Christiana quæ est sponsa & corpus Christi. Sit istorum igitur error & cavillatio fallacia dictionis. Preterea aliud est esse in Ecclesia visibili, viderique de Ecclesia Catholica illa esse: aliud verè esse de Ecclesia Catholica: hoc est, reuera Christi membrum esse. Fallaciam etiam admittunt in vocabulo Reprobi per æquiuocationem. Nam Reprobos confundunt cum Improbis & peccatoribus: quum tamen proprie Reprobi dicantur illi qui sunt exitio æterno afficiendi. Fideles sunt quidem peccatores: & multi eorum qui sunt seruandi, siue qui vera sunt Ecclesiæ veræ & corporis Christi membra, sæpe sunt aliquandiu Improbi, qui tamen nequaquam sunt Reprobi.
units.tr: In the fourth chapter of the earlier Analysis, Arturus tries to refute the argument, bringing forward much about the Reprobate in order to prove that they belong to the Catholic Church, which is the body and spouse of Christ. He pursues this at length from chapter 10 to chapter 13 of the first book, and in chapter 2 of the second book. This objection, however, was treated at length against Turrianus in the Index, articles 16, 17 and 25, and in the reply against him. The sophisms he repeats here are refuted in the first writing at article 8, in the eighth writing at articles 9, 10, 12 and 13, and throughout the tenth writing, where everything Arturus brings forward on this matter, merely following in the footsteps of Turrianus, is refuted. These points need not be repeated here. Arturus, however, sophistically substitutes an exclamation for a reply. So at p. 60 he cries out in Greek and Latin, "O sycophant [ὦ συκοφάντα] ... O fictitious refuge! O invention! O paradox!" But if it pleased me to imitate that ridiculous exclaimer and declaimer, with what words should we receive those who, in order to prove that the Roman Church is the Church of Christ and that a single visible head must be set over it, contend that the Reprobate belong to it! Who, as if pleading the cause of the Reprobate, blasphemously assert that they are members of Christ! Are they not compelled to acknowledge that there is one Christ, the life-giving head of the Catholic Church? Moreover, in this question Arturus and his other companions use a metaphor [μεταφορά], a transposition of the words IN and OF, as a trick. For it has never been denied that the Reprobate are in visible churches; this is plain. But it is denied that the Reprobate are of the Christian Church, which is the spouse and body of Christ. So let their error and quibbling be called a fallacy of expression. Furthermore, to be in the visible Church is one thing, and to seem to be of that Catholic Church is another; to truly be of the Catholic Church, that is, to really be a member of Christ, is yet a third. They also admit a fallacy through equivocation in the word Reprobi. For they confuse the Reprobate with the wicked and with sinners, whereas those are properly called Reprobate who are destined for eternal destruction. The faithful are indeed sinners, and many of those who are to be saved, or who are true members of the true Church and of the body of Christ, are often wicked for some time, yet by no means Reprobate.

units.la: CAPVT. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: ARTVRVS toto libro secundo suarum Responsionum caput 5. de Notis Ecclesiæ superioris Analysis oppugnat. Ac primum quidē hoc proponit. Vix, inquit, visum teneba, quū legerem proponendū esse de qua Ecclesia sermonem haberem, quasi plures sint in terris Christi Ecclesiae. Risus ille Sardonius est,Arturc.Renera vna est Christi Ecclesia:sed omnes illam sibi vendicát.Iudæi & Turcę populum fe Dei nominant:Iefuitę faciunt Ecclesiam perfectorum,sic & reliqui monachi,vt & Anabaptistæ: Pontificij hæretici nomen Ecclesiæ suffurantur. Recte igitur dicebatur tum in super.Analysi:cum aduersus Turrianü loco script. 1. proponendam esse Ecclesiæ legitimā definitionem,vt vera Ecclesia à falsa discerna- tur statuaturque de qua Ecclesia habeatur sermo.Pergit Arturus inquiens: Ecclesia est aspe- ctabilis: ergo illius nota debent esse aspectabiles. Sincera prædicatio & legitimus Sacramentorum vsus in sola Christi Ecclesia reperitur quidem : sed non sunt tamen ipsius nota. Idem enim per idem de- monstratur:vt siquis rogatus viam quæ ducit Thebis Athenas,respondeat eam esse quæ ducit Athenis Thebas: Et debuit Sadeel sic conficere argumentationem ex meis thesibus. Quicunque statuunt eas Ecclesiæ notas quæ sunt ipsa Ecclesia obscuriores, communes,friuolæ,ignorant quid sit Ecclesia & penes quos existat. Tales aduersarij asignant. Ignorant igitur vbi sit Ecclesia. Illa demum multitudo & congregatio est Ecclesia quæ veritatem tenet. Vera autem Ecclesia demonstrāda est notis essentialibus. At Monachi accidentarias Ecclesiæ proferunt notas, cum reliquis Congregationum generibus communes: vt siquis ignoret quænam sint Athenæ aut Thebę viam quærat, quæ Thebis Athenas: & contrà Athenis Thebas : accidentibus vt Monachi adhærescit. Verbum autem Dei & Ecclesia res eadem non est:sed illud est mensura,hæc est vt mensumensuratum: Non igitur idem per idem demonstratur, quum ex verbo Dei Ecclesia Dei in terris demonstratur.
units.tr: Arturus, in the second book of his Responses, chapter 5, attacks the above Analysis of the marks of the Church. And first he puts forward this: "I scarcely thought," he says, "when I read that we must first propose which Church we are discussing, that there are several Churches of Christ on earth." That is a sardonic laugh. Arturus, there is only one Church of Christ, but everyone claims it for themselves. The Jews and the Turks call themselves the people of God. The Jesuits make themselves the Church of the perfect, as do the other monks, and the Anabaptists too. The Papists, being heretics, steal the name of Church. Rightly, then, was it said in the above Analysis, when against Turrianus in the first book it was argued that a lawful definition of the Church must be set out, so that the true Church may be distinguished from the false and it may be settled which Church is meant. Arturus goes on: "The Church is visible; therefore its marks must be visible. The sincere preaching and lawful use of the sacraments are indeed found only in the true Church of Christ, but they are not its marks. For this is to prove the same thing by the same thing, as if someone asked the way that leads from Thebes to Athens and answered that it is the road that leads from Athens to Thebes. And Sadeel ought to have framed his argument from my theses thus: Whoever set up as marks of the Church things more obscure than the Church itself, common and trivial, do not know what the Church is or where it exists. Such are the opponents. Therefore they do not know where the Church is." That multitude and congregation is the Church which holds the truth. But the true Church must be shown by its essential marks. The Monks, however, put forward accidental marks of the Church, which are common to other kinds of congregation, so that if someone does not know what Athens or Thebes is, he must seek the road that leads from Thebes to Athens, and conversely from Athens to Thebes, since it clings to accidents, as the monks do. But the Word of God and the Church are not the same thing: the one is the rule, the other is what is measured by the rule. So the same thing is not proved by the same thing, when the Church of God on earth is shown from the Word of God.

units.la: Nam quum quaeritur cui multitudini convenient nomen Ecclesiae: respondendum est illam demum multitudinem & congregationem verè Christi Ecclesiam esse quae veritatem retinet in verbo Dei patefactam. Haec enim est differentia specifica ut vera in terris Ecclesia secernatur ab aliis congregationibus illud nomen falsò sibi vindicantibus. Caeterum Argumentatio iltius Assertoris melius structa fuit in superiore Analysi, ex legibus rite differendi, quàm ipse nunc eam proponat. Nam quamuis eodem recidat argumentatio: tamen iste mutat terminos: & plures reperiuntur quàm tres termini in iltius syllogizandi impericia ratione.
units.tr: For when it is asked to which multitude the name Church belongs, the answer must be that the multitude and congregation which retains the truth revealed in the Word of God is truly the Church of Christ. For this is the specific difference, by which the true Church on earth is set apart from other congregations that falsely claim that name for themselves. Otherwise, the argument of that opponent was better constructed in the above Analysis, according to the rules of right reasoning, than he now sets it out. For although the argument comes to the same thing, yet he changes the terms, and in the unskilled way of his syllogizing there are more than three terms.

units.la: Cap.2.lib.sui secundi, pergit oppugnare signa illa & notas illas essentiales verae Christi Ecclesiae assignatas, nempe Synceram verbi Dei praedicationem & rectum usum Sacramentorum, quia, inquit, carent proprietatibus signorum. Nam signa debent esse evidentia & ἀχωρίστα ex Augusti. ut Ducum vexilla & Cimutatum insignia & Principum sigilla: alioqui non sunt τὰ ἀνώτερα aut σημεῖα ἀναλυτικά. At sincera praedicatio & legitimus sacramentorum usus sunt res obscurae: & ipsae Scripturae sunt difficiles intellectu. Sunt enim mysteria & res arcanae. Ergo illa non sunt signa Ecclesiae evidentia. Nec sunt etiam ἀχωρίστα. Nam multae Ecclesiae pro veris habitae sunt, quibus tum sincera verbi Dei praedicatio tum legitimus Sacra-
units.tr: In chapter 2 of his second book he goes on to attack those signs and essential marks of the true Church that were assigned, namely the pure preaching of the Word of God and the right use of the sacraments, "because," he says, "they lack the properties of signs. For signs must be evident and inseparable, according to Augustine, like the banners of commanders, the badges of the cities, and the seals of princes; otherwise they are not τὰ ἀνώτερα [superior things] or σημεῖα ἀναλυτικά [analytic signs]. But the sincere preaching and lawful use of the sacraments are obscure things, and the Scriptures themselves are hard to understand, for they are mysteries and hidden matters. Therefore they are not evident signs of the Church. Nor are they inseparable. For many churches have been regarded as true in which the sincere preaching of the Word of God and the lawful use of the sacra-

units.la: C. iiij. mentorum vsus defuit, vt Ecclesia Corinthiorum & Galatarum. Sad eel etiam mutat quaestionis statum. Non enim hic de essentia Ecclesiae agitur, neque quid sit Ecclesia quaeritur, sed quana & penes quos existat. Quia iam satis multa de notis Ecclesiae tum in super. Analysi, tum aduersus Tur. loco 1. Art. 30. & loco. 10. Art. 3. dicta sunt, paucis erit huic respondendum: ipsum abuti vocabulo signi, quod hic no in ea significatione sumitur, qua Augustinus signa sacramentalia explicat. Sed hic, signa, Notae & Conditiones Ecclesiae essentiales, & τημεια pro vno eodemque vsurpantur: adeo vt ille frustra laboret in assignandis Signorum proprietatibus ex accidentibus petitis. Quod si quaeramus quaenam & penes quos existat Ecclesia, vt ille ait, omnino quaerimus quid sit Ecclesia: nec mutatur quaestio. Τημεῖον autem non semper in oculos incurrit: Rei natura spectanda est mentis oculis. Definitur Ecclesia, fidelium congregatio: tenendum est quid sit fidelem esse. Nam ipsi homines sunt alpectabiles, & ipsa congregatio videtur & incurrit in sensus: Quomodo igitur scias vbi sit Ecclesia & penes quos existat, nisi scias quid sit? Ex quo perspicitur fidelibus solis (ad quos pertinet Ecclesia) euidentes esse illas Ecclesiae notas, quas posuimus. Fides enim dirigit oculos ad veram Dei Ecclesiam cognoscendam: quae verbum Domini tanquam lucernam sibi proponit. Ex quo ita colligendum est: Oues, hoc est, Ecclesia Christi, sunt qui cunque vocem eius audiunt: retinentque sincerum verbi Dei praedicationem & legitimum SaSacramentorum vsum: quæ non sunt ipsis signa obscura, vt isti aiunt qui Ecclesiā metiuntur accidentibus: cuiusmodi sunt Multitudo & Diffusio. Cuiusmodi autem est Congregatio, eiusmodi est forma essentialis, signáque sunt ipsius quærenda: nec adhærescendum accidentibus χωρίσοις quæ & adesse & abesse possunt, & quæ solis oculis corporeis perspiciuntur.
units.tr: ments were lacking, such as the Church of the Corinthians and of the Galatians." Sadeel also changes the state of the question. For the question here is not about the essence of the Church, nor what the Church is, but where and among whom it exists. Since enough has already been said about the marks of the Church, both in the above Analysis and against Turrianus, book 1, article 30, and book 10, article 3, a few words will be enough in reply. He misuses the word "sign", which here is not taken in the sense in which Augustine explains sacramental signs. Here "signs", "marks", and the essential conditions of the Church, and τημεῖα [signs] are used as one and the same thing, so that he labours in vain to assign properties of signs drawn from accidents. And if we ask what the Church is and where and among whom it exists, as he says, we are altogether asking what the Church is, and the question is not changed. But a τημεῖον [sign] does not always strike the eyes; the nature of the thing must be looked at with the eyes of the mind. The Church is defined as the congregation of believers; we must consider what it is to be a believer. For men themselves are visible, and the congregation itself is seen and falls under the senses. How then can you know where the Church is and among whom it exists, unless you know what it is? From this it is clear that those marks which we have set out are evident to believers alone, to whom the Church belongs. For faith directs the eyes to recognise the true Church of God, which holds the Word of the Lord before itself as a lamp. From this the conclusion must be drawn thus: the sheep, that is, the Church of Christ, are all who hear his voice and hold to the sincere preaching of the Word of God and the lawful use of the sacraments. These are not obscure signs for them, as those say who measure the Church by accidents, such as multitude and extent. But what sort of congregation it is, that is the sort of essential form it has, and its signs must be sought from that; nor must one cling to accidents, which are separable (χωρίσοις [separable]) and can both be present and absent, and which are perceived only by the bodily eyes.

units.la: Cæterum instantia de Ecclesiis Corinthiorum, Galatarum, & similibus, à Turriano propósita & ab Arturo repósita: nequaquam labefactat illas conditiones Ecclesiæ essentiales, sine quibus non esset amplius Ecclesia nisi æquivocè, vt homo pictus dicitur homo. Errores multi quidem in Ecclesiis particularibus sæpius surrepunt: qui tamen sunt distinguendi: sunt enim quidam errores qui fundamenta doctrinæ Euangelicæ tollunt: tunc vbi errores illi obtinent, reiectâ verâ doctrinâ, ibi nö amplius est Ecclesia Christi. Deinde distinguendum est, quando illi errores Ecclesiæ alicuius partes omnes occupauerunt: adeò vt tota Ecclesia errores amplectatur qui fundamenta fidei totámque doctrinam ad salutem conuelunt: & quando nonnulli tantum prauis illis erroribus sunt imbuti, adeò vt maneat tamen Ecclesia propter reliquos qui sanam doctrinâ retinent. Non enim valet argumentum à parte ad euertendum totum: vt si multi sint qui non retinent doctrinam syncerăm: non hinc statim est colligendum, totam Ecclesiam etiam defecisse. Ideo apud Corinthios & Galatas
units.tr: Moreover, the objection about the Churches of the Corinthians, the Galatians, and similar churches, put forward by Turrianus and answered by Arturus, does not in any way weaken those essential conditions of the Church, without which it would no longer be a Church except equivocally, as a painted man is called a man. Many errors indeed often creep into particular churches, but these must be distinguished. For some errors overthrow the foundations of evangelical doctrine; where such errors prevail and the true doctrine is rejected, there is no longer the Church of Christ. Next, we must distinguish when those errors have taken hold of all parts of a church, so that the whole church embraces errors that overthrow the foundations of faith and the whole doctrine of salvation, and when only some have been imbued with those pernicious errors, so that the church nevertheless remains because of the rest who hold sound doctrine. For an argument from a part cannot overthrow the whole: if there are many who do not hold sincere doctrine, it does not follow at once that the whole Church has also fallen away.

units.la: dicit Apostolus fuisse etiam inter illos dissidia, hæreses esse inter illos. Ergo non omnes defecerant: quos etiam Apostolus vocat fratres. Et ad Galatas dicit. Paulum fermenti totam massam fermentat:vtinam abscindantnr qui vos inquietat. Non omnes igitur doctrinam abiecerant, sed eos admonet Apostolus vt mature sibi prospiciant ne cum reliquis deficiant. Erat igitur inter illos Ecclesia,quæ quidem à meliori parte sic denominatur.
units.tr: So the Apostle says of the Corinthians that "there were also divisions among them, there were heresies among them." Therefore not all had fallen away; the Apostle even calls them brothers. And to the Galatians he says: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump; I wish that those who trouble you would cut themselves off." Therefore not all had rejected the doctrine, but the Apostle warns them to look to themselves in time, lest they fall away with the rest. There was therefore a Church among them, which is rightly named after the better part.

units.la: Ex his etiam euenitur altera istius Instantia Excommunicatum ab Ecclesia, inquit, non solum credimus ,sed videmus : ex quo vult colligere, notas Ecclesiæ debere visibiles esse. Et nos etiam in Ecclesiis particularibus fideles videmus: sed quibus oculis errorem in doctrina discernimus, iisdem veram doctrinam videmus. Aures corporeæ audiunt ipsam doctrinam: sed animus suis ad id qualitatibus idoneis præditus, de ea diiudicat. Excommunicantur autem refractarij propter improbitatem vulgò notam.Sed quid hoc ad notas Ecclesiæ essentiales? Nam ad differentiam specificam veniendum est, vt cœtus & congregationes secernantur: quum multa sint genera cœtuum & congregationum. Vnde necessario colligitur Ecclesiam penes eos & apud eos esse vbi vexillum sinceræ prædicationis & Sacramentorum elatû est ex verbi Dei præscripto: quod quidem verbum Dei scriptum tam clarè & aperte fidei Articulos proponit, vt extremæ sit impietatis co nomine illud dicere obscurum. Et sane apertior est Scriptura sacra & facilior quàm sint scripta Veterû, qui inter se & à sei-psis sæpe dissident. At sacra Scriptura tota est sibi cohærens & συμφωνος, quâ & nobis cû a-guosc̅unt Pontificij. Hanc Augustin. & reliqui pii Veteres aduersus hæreticos proferebat: nec ad Traditiones ἀγράφως recurrebant. Sacræ au-tem Scripturæ claritissimam esse docent perspi-cuitatem, scripta veterum Ecclesiæ doctorum, aduersus illos tenebriones, qui luce verbi Dei conantur obscurare. Chrysost. hom. 21. in Gen.
units.tr: From this also comes the other objection of that opponent: "We believe not only that someone is excommunicated from the Church, but we see it." From this he wants to conclude that the marks of the Church ought to be visible. And we too see believers in particular churches; but by the same eyes by which we discern error in doctrine, we see the true doctrine as well. Bodily ears hear the doctrine itself, but the mind, endowed with qualities suited to this, judges of it. Those who are obstinate are excommunicated on account of their wickedness, which is commonly known. But what has this to do with the essential marks of the Church? For we must come to the specific difference, so that assemblies and congregations may be distinguished, since there are many kinds of assemblies and congregations. Hence it is necessarily concluded that the Church is where and among those who have raised the banner of the sincere preaching and of the sacraments according to the precept of the Word of God; and this written Word of God sets forth the articles of faith so clearly and openly that it is the height of impiety to call it obscure on that account. And indeed Holy Scripture is more open and easier than the writings of the ancients, who often disagree with one another and with themselves. But Holy Scripture is wholly consistent with itself and συμφωνος [in agreement], as even the Papists acknowledge. Augustine and the other godly ancients used it against the heretics, and did not have recourse to unwritten traditions [ἀγράφως]. Writings of the ancient teachers of the Church teach that Holy Scripture has the clearest perspicuity, against those darkeners who try to obscure it with the light of God's Word. Chrysostom, homily 21 on Genesis.

units.la: Non eget diuina Scriptura hominum sapientia ut intelligatur. In Ef. cap. 2. Quod lumen est oculo, id est Lex Dei menti nostræ: Ergo non est obscura, ut isti autumant, alioqui non esset lux. In Matth. hom. 2. Hoc est quod omnia communi peste corrumpit quod lectione Scripturarum ad solos Monachos putatis pertinere. In proœ. in Ep. ad Rom. Vt qui lucis huius visura non fruuntur, recta ingredi non possunt: ita qui ad Scripturæ radios, oculos non intendunt, in multos errores necessario incidut. Exorta sunt mala ab ipsa Scripturarum ignoratione. Athanas. ad Serap. Ne interroges, sed solum ex sacris literis condiscas. Sufficiunt enim quæ in illis reperias documenta. or. 2. de Incar. Ecce iam nos ex sacris literis fideliter loquimur de religiosa & pia fide & quasi candelam super candelabrum collocantes, hæc pronuntiamus. Augustin. de Trin. lib. 1. S. Scriptura parvulis congruens. Ep. 3. Modus dicendi quo S. Scriptura contexitur omnibus accessibilis. Sent. 120. Sicut stellas non extinguit nox: sic mentes fidelium firmamento adhærentes sanctæ Scripturæ non obscurat mundana iniquitas. Epist. 3. Tanta est profunditas Christianarum literarum,
units.tr: Divine Scripture does not need human wisdom in order to be understood. In Ef. cap. 2. What the light is to the eye, the Law of God is to our mind. Therefore it is not obscure, as these men claim; otherwise it would not be light. In Matth. hom. 2. This is what corrupts everything with a common plague: you think that the reading of the Scriptures belongs only to monks. In proœ. in Ep. ad Rom. Those who do not enjoy this light cannot walk straight; so those who do not turn their eyes to the rays of Scripture necessarily fall into many errors. Evils have arisen from ignorance of the Scriptures themselves. Athanas. ad Serap. Do not ask questions, but learn only from the holy letters. For the teachings you find in them are enough. or. 2. de Incar. See, we now speak faithfully from the holy letters about the religious and pious faith, and, setting the lamp on the lampstand, we proclaim these things. Augustin. de Trin. lib. 1. Holy Scripture is suited to little children. Ep. 3. The manner of speaking in which Holy Scripture is woven is accessible to all. Sent. 120. As night does not extinguish the stars, so the worldly wickedness does not obscure holy Scripture to the minds of the faithful who cling to its firmament. Epist. 3. So great is the depth of Christian letters,

units.la: illegible margin notes not reliably read vt in eis annosissimi, acutissimi, flagratissimique cupiditate discendi quotidie proficiant. Non quo ad ea quae sunt necessaria saluti, tanta in eis peruemniatur difficultate. libr. 83. quaest. 53. Deus ad salutem sic diuinos libros moderatus est: vt in manifestis nos pascat, & obscuris exercere nos velit. De doctr. Chr. lib. 2. In iis quae aperte in Scriptura posita sunt, illa omnia inueniuntur quae continent fidem morésque viuendi: quae. ex vtroque mixtum 109. Quae est tam versuta ingenij calliditas quae audet resistere manifestis vt non sensum capiat ex lectione, sed sensum tribuat lectioni? Ambrosius, Sanctis Scripturis non loquentibus quis loquetur? Epiphanius. Omnia clara sunt in diuina Scriptura iis qui pia ratiocinatione diuinum sermonem adire volunt, contra Anomaeos. Nihil est in diuina Scriptura obliquum, nihil tortuosum, sed omnia mirabiliter ad nostram salutem scripta sunt & perfecta. cont. Ariom. Adde ea quae de hac re in tract. de Verbo Dei scripto. Conticescant igitur Arturi & reliquorum Monachorum obiectiones blasphemae de obscuritate verbi diuini per quod diuina voluntas nobis innotescit. Nec minus blasphema vox est Arturi illa qua negat Verbum Dei scriptum esse μίτρον fidei cap. 3. lib. 2. sui. Et ad hanc blasphemiam comprobandam parum commode citat locos quosdam ex patribus, vbi commendant Traditiones. Nam illi loquuntur de Traditionibus quae ex Scriptura sacra haustae sunt: vt quū Ambrosius ait: Symbolum Apostolorum esse traditionem non scriptam. Citat etiam Arturus Augustinum qui ait: Sunt libri Canonici quorum auctoauctoritati vtrique consentimus, vtrique credimus, vtrique seruimus, ibi quaeramus Ecclesiam, ibi didiscutiamus causam nostram lib. de vnitate Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: illegible margin notes not reliably read that the most aged, the most acute and the most ardent in eager desire to learn make progress in them daily. Not that such great difficulty is encountered in them concerning the things that are necessary for salvation. libr. 83. quaest. 53. God has so tempered the divine books for our salvation that he feeds us in the plain passages and wishes to exercise us in the obscure ones. De doctr. Chr. lib. 2. In those things which are set down plainly in Scripture, all those things are found which contain faith and the rules of living. Quae. from both mixed, 109. What cleverness of wit is so crafty that it dares to resist plain statements, so as not to take the sense from the reading, but to impose a sense on the reading? Ambrose, When the holy Scriptures do not speak, who will speak? Epiphanius. Everything is clear in divine Scripture to those who wish to approach the divine word with pious reasoning, against the Anomoeans. Nothing in divine Scripture is crooked, nothing tortuous, but everything has been written wonderfully and perfectly for our salvation. against Arians. Add what is said on this matter in the treatise on the written Word of God. Let the blasphemous objections of Artur and of the other monks about the obscurity of the divine Word, through which the divine will is made known to us, therefore fall silent. Artur's saying, by which he denies that the written Word of God is the rule [μέτρον] of faith, bk. 2, ch. 3 of his book, is no less blasphemous. And to prove this blasphemy he cites, rather inappropriately, certain passages from the Fathers where they commend Traditions. For they speak of Traditions that were drawn from holy Scripture, as when Ambrose says: The Apostles' Creed is an unwritten tradition. Artur also cites Augustine, who says: There are canonical books, to whose authority we both agree, both believe, both serve; there let us seek the Church, there let us examine our cause. From the book on the unity of the Church.

units.la: Rursus Arturus negat, cap.4. p. 113. Ecclesiam esse effectum verbi Dei scripti: quum ante verbum Dei scriptum fuerit. Ecclesia, inquit, Et diuinæ literæ clarius de Ecclesia quam de dogmatibus fidei loquuntur, Affirmo igitur (inquit ille) Ecclesiam posse cognosci absque verbo Dei: hoc est, absque cognitione sincera prædicationis omnium dogmatum Christianæ religionis. Omnia falsa, posterius hoc quoque captiosum. Nam S. Scriptura diserte affirmat id quod iste impure negat: Sic enim Ioannes. Hæc scripta sunt vt credatis. Et Apostolus. Placuit Deo per prædicationem seruare credentes. Item: Discatis supra id quod scriptum est non sapere. 1.Cor.4. Ef.8. Ad legem & ad testimonium: si non dixerint iuxta hoc verbum nihil habent lucis. 2. Tim. 3. A puero sacras literas nosti quæ te possunt sapientem reddere ad salutem, &c. Porrò nos loquimur de Ecclesia quæ nunc & temporibus hisce extruenda est super doctrinam à Prophetis & Apostolis conscriptam. Olim & Nunc discrimen statuunt: hoc est, temporum distinctio illam tollunt cauillationem. Nos enim verba facimus de Ecclesia quæ hisce temporibus est ex Verbo Dei scripto constituenda, in quo fidei dogmata clarissimè proponuntur. Captiosum quoque est hoc quod Arturus ad finem attexit de prædicatione sincera omnium dogmatum religionis. Nos enim loquimur non de vno dogmate, sed de dogmatibus religionis Christianæ fundamentalibus, sine quibus, nec est vera religio, nec Ecclesia Christiana vera. Et hæc Ecclesia quomodo docebit nisi ex Scriptura? vt docet Augustinus epist. 166. quem ille inscienter aduersus se citauit.
units.tr: Again Artur, ch. 4, p. 113, denies that the Church is the effect of the written Word of God, since the Church existed before the written Word of God. The Church, he says, and the divine letters speak more clearly of the Church than of the doctrines of faith. I affirm, therefore, he says, that the Church can be known without the Word of God, that is, without sincere knowledge of the preaching of all the doctrines of the Christian religion. All these statements are false, and the last one is also deceptive. For holy Scripture expressly affirms what he impudently denies. Thus John: These things are written that you may believe. And the Apostle: It pleased God to save believers through preaching. Likewise: Learn not to think beyond what is written. 1 Cor. 4. Eph. 8. To the law and to the testimony: if they do not speak according to this word, they have no light. 2 Tim. 3. From childhood you have known the holy letters, which can make you wise unto salvation, etc. Moreover, we are speaking of the Church, which now, in these times, is to be built upon the doctrine written down by the Prophets and Apostles. Artur makes a distinction between then and now; that is, the distinction of times removes that quibble. For we are speaking of the Church, which in these times is to be constituted from the written Word of God, in which the articles of faith are most clearly set forth. What Artur adds at the end, about the sincere preaching of all the doctrines of religion, is also deceptive. For we are speaking not of one doctrine but of the fundamental doctrines of the Christian religion, without which there is neither true religion nor a true Christian Church. And how will this Church teach unless from Scripture? As Augustine teaches in epist. 166, whom he foolishly cited against us.

units.la: Non concedam iactationem Sadeelis, inquit, Arturus, Ecclesiæ notas esse illas quas profert. Nam hæretici eas sibi vendicant & ipse Diabolus. Matt. 4. Sunt igitur Notæ communes: ac proinde non sunt propriæ Ecclesiæ notæ. Hæc illæ, cap. 5 lib. 2. quæ non dicenda sunt de illis Notis essentialibus: sed de Notis accidentariis: Multitudine, Diffusione, Consuetudine confirmata vetustate, quas Ariani, Turcæ, Iudæi, &c. iactant. Christus autem non opponit Satanæ auctoritatem Ecclesiæ, sed ipsum Dei verbum, Matt. 4. nos erudiens quomodo nos gerere debeamus aduersus eos qui S. Scriptura abutentes, à vero Dei cultu nos reuocare studeant. Ar, inquit ille: hæretici falsò Scripturam sibi vendicant. Nos igitur vere & vt par est, ea nobis applicemus quod est proprium fidelium, ac proinde veræ Christi Ecclesiæ. Insipientia autem istorum qui pseudoecclesiam tuentur est manifesta, vt ait Apostolus, 2. Tim. 3. non vt Arturus cum locum citat. Sic enim Apostolus: Insipientia eorum erit manifesta. Arturus autem hic locum citat: Insipientia eorum erat manifesta: quasi iam non possint pontificiorum errores esse manifesti.
units.tr: I do not grant, says Artur, the boast of Sadeel that those are the marks of the Church which he produces. For heretics claim them for themselves, and the Devil himself. Matt. 4. Therefore these are common marks, and consequently they are not proper marks of the Church. These are his words, ch. 5, bk. 2; but they should not be said of those essential marks, only of the accidental marks: multitude, extent, custom, and antiquity confirmed by age, which the Arians, Turks, Jews, etc. boast of. Christ, however, does not set against Satan the authority of the Church, but the Word of God itself, Matt. 4, teaching us how we ought to act against those who, abusing holy Scripture, strive to call us back from the true worship of God. Heretics, he says, falsely claim Scripture for themselves. We therefore, truly and as is fitting, apply to ourselves that which is proper to believers, and consequently to the true Church of Christ. The folly of those who defend the false church is manifest, as the Apostle says, 2 Tim. 3, not as Artur quotes the place. For the Apostle says: Their folly will be manifest. Artur, however, here cites the passage as: Their folly was manifest, as if the errors of the Papists could no longer be made manifest.

units.la: Cap. 6. & 7. & 8. libr. 2. Arturus ait, falsum esse: Maiores nostros ex diuino verbo confodisse hæreticos: qui figmenta sua pro Scripturis obtrudebant bant:vt modo Lutherani & Caluiniani obtrudunt, inquit.Hoc vt probet, proferr impudentissimas calumnias:aduersus Lutherum, Caluinū, &c. quas ex sui similibus sycophantis corradit.Ad quæ nihil præterea respondendum,nisi putidissima esse medacia: & nihil eorum quæ illi volunt inde concludi.Subiicit: Nullos Patres nullaque Concilia verbum Dei scriptum pro Ecclesia nota vsurpasse. At hoc est fallissimum, nisi hoc Arturus de Tridentino Conciliabulo &similibus Pontificis Synodis intelligar.Contrà nos affirmamus omnia Concilia orthodoxa & patres pios Veteres,Scripturam sacrā adhibuisse, vt veram Ecclesiam, veramque doctrinam à falsa discernerent:ac inde hæreticos refutasse,quòd doctrinā Scripturæ repugnantem proferrent.Proponebant hæretici, inquit Irenæus,non verbum Dei scriptum sed inanes & falsas traditiones quas ad Apostolos falsò referrebant. Vera Christi Ecclesia quomodo docebit, nisi ex Dei verbo? Pij etiam veteres nolunt sibi fidem haberi,nisi docceant consentanea Scripturis.Sed secum ipse pugnat Arturus qui supra agnouerit nos Scripturas nobis vendicare. Perperam autem concluditur: figmenta pro Scripturis obtrudunt hæretici: Ergo Scriptura non est Nota Ecclesiæ. Deinde sunt-ne hæc consectaria? Vos solis nitimini Scripturis: &, nihil nisi purum verbum Dei recipitis. Ergo vos sectamini figmenta hæreticorum:imo impia est hæc colligendi ratio.At, inquit Arturus,nonne hæretici collatione Scripturarum occurrebant Catholicis.Nam quum Catholici afferebant pro ὁμοουσίῳ,Ego & Pater vnum sumus, haretici proferebant contra: Oro vt vnum sint, sicut tu Pater in me, &c. Ergo, verbi diuini sententia non semper certo colligitur ex locis Scripturae collatis. Nonne Vbiquitarij, Lutherani & Anabaptistae conferunt Scripturas. Itaque ad Concilia patres confugerunt: quae Concilia non notas Ecclesiae vsurparunt, quas Sadeel profert, &c. Reste igitur Augustinus contra Epist. fund. c. 5. Euangelio non crederem, nisi me Catholicae Ecclesiae commoneret auctoritas. Haec Arturus cap. 7. & 8. l. 2.
units.tr: Chs. 6, 7 and 8 of bk. 2. Artur says it is false that our forefathers refuted heretics from the divine Word, who foisted their own inventions on us as Scripture, as the Lutherans and Calvinists now do. To prove this he brings forward the most shameless calumnies against Luther, Calvin, etc., which he has scraped together from sycophants like himself. To these nothing more need be answered than that they are most foul lies, and nothing that he wishes to conclude from them follows. He adds: No Fathers and no Councils have ever used the written Word of God as a recognized mark of the Church. But this is most false, unless Artur means the Tridentine conventicle and similar synods of the Pope. On the contrary, we affirm that all orthodox Councils and the pious ancient Fathers used holy Scripture to distinguish the true Church and true doctrine from the false, and thereby refuted heretics because they put forward doctrine contrary to Scripture. The heretics, says Irenaeus, put forward not the written Word of God but empty and false traditions, which they falsely traced back to the Apostles. How will the true Church of Christ teach, unless from the Word of God? The pious ancients also did not wish to be believed unless they taught what agrees with Scripture. But Artur contradicts himself, since above he acknowledged that we claim Scriptures for ourselves. Moreover, he wrongly concludes: heretics foist inventions upon us as Scripture; therefore Scripture is not a mark of the Church. Further, do these follow? You rely on Scriptures alone and receive nothing but the pure Word of God; therefore you follow the inventions of heretics. Indeed, this way of drawing conclusions is impious. But, says Artur, did not the heretics, by comparing Scriptures, meet the Catholics? For when the Catholics brought forward, for the homoousion [ὁμοουσίῳ], "I and the Father are one," the heretics answered with: "that they may be one, as you, Father, are in me," etc. Therefore the sense of the divine word is not always surely gathered from comparing passages of Scripture. Do not the Ubiquitarians, Lutherans and Anabaptists compare Scriptures? Therefore they fled to the Fathers and the Councils, which Councils did not claim the marks of the Church that Sadeel produces, etc. Rightly therefore Augustine, against the fundamental epistle, ch. 5: I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me. Thus Artur, ch. 7 and 8, bk. 2.

units.la: Aliud est conferre, aliud opponere. Locis S. Scripturae occurrebant haeretici, non vt conferrent, sed vt opponeret Scripturam Scripturae quae tota est αὐτάλληλος: Pij autem Maiores illas haereticorum expositiones redarguebant: tum ex locorum circumstantiis: tum adductis aliis locis clarissimis. Nec sequitur: Plerique male conferunt, vt Pontificij, Vbiquitarij, Anabaptistae, Ariani. Ergo, S. Scripturae interpretatio genuina non est depromenda ex legitima locorum collatione. Aliud est bene conferre; aliud, male conferre: Item, sie Scripturae addicere: & addicere Scripturam sibi plurimum differunt. Sed ille putat, proferre Scripturam, sed conferre locos Scripturae: quasi ἐξήγησις sit ἐξηγήσεως.
units.tr: To compare is one thing, to oppose is another. Heretics came upon the passages of Holy Scripture not to compare them but to set Scripture against Scripture, although the whole of Scripture is αὐτάλληλος [self-consistent]. The pious Fathers, however, refuted those heretical interpretations, both from the circumstances of the passages and by adducing other, very clear passages. Nor does it follow: many compare badly, as the Papists, Ubiquitarians, Anabaptists and Arians do; therefore the genuine interpretation of Holy Scripture is not to be drawn from a lawful comparison of passages. To compare well is one thing, to compare badly another. Likewise, to bend Scripture to oneself and to bend oneself to Scripture are very different things. But he thinks that to bring forward Scripture is the same as to compare passages of Scripture, as if exposition [ἐξήγησις] were the same as the genitive of exposition [ἐξηγήσεως].

units.la: Quod ad locum Augustini attinet quem vulgo solent Pontificij nobis obiicere, Sententia Augustini haec est: Consensum Ecclesiae (qualis tum erat Ecclesia multis ornamentis conspicua) plurimum posse ad commouendos rudiorum animos, qui tum demum credunt, quum in Ecclesia docentur ex verbo Dei, credidisse autem se dicit Augustinus, quia edoctus fuit ab Ecclesia: nempe ut ait Apostolus Rom. 10. fides est ex auditu verbi Dei. Ex quo efficitur Ecclesiam id praestare, quum docet ex Verbo Dei. Ergo, nos non credimus nisi ex Verbo Dei doceamur, quae res est sententiae nostrae confirmatio: & vera Augustini sententia, qui etiam ibi loquitur ex hypothesi de infidelibus qui ad credendum commouentur Ecclesiae auctoritate: ut Ioan. 4. Multi crediderunt propter sermonem mulieris, qui postea mulieri dicebant, Non amplius propter sermones tuos credimus: ipsi enim audiimus & scimus hunc esse vere Seruatorem mundi. Apud infirmos quidem maior videtur esse Ecclesiae authoritas: quae tamen non est in sese maior, quam verbi divini scripti auctoritas. At nos credimus Euangelio de quo non dubitamus. Vera autem Ecclesia Scripturam fideliter proponit: & ita Ecclesiae authoritas nos commouet. Veteres Patres hanc rationem afferebant, Ecclesiam nimirum esse fundatam in Scriptura: atque hinc omnes haereticos, ex Scripturis videlicet, refutabant. Quid diiudicaut Nicaenum ab Ariminensi Concilio nisi Scriptura? Sic Patres illi pij in Conciliis legitimis proferebant Scripturam aduersus haereticos ut in doctrina Apostolorum persecuerant: nec illis nudum nomen Ecclesiae opponebant. Refutabantur haeretici, & hodie sic sunt refutandi, quia doctrinam incognitam ac proinde Scripturae sacrae repugnantem profitentur.
units.tr: As for the passage of Augustine which the Papists usually throw at us, the sense of Augustine is this: the consensus of the Church (such as the Church then was, distinguished by many ornaments) has great power to move the minds of the less learned, who only then believe when they are taught in the Church from the Word of God. Augustine says that he believed because he was taught by the Church, namely, as the Apostle says in Romans 10, faith comes from hearing the Word of God. From this it follows that the Church accomplishes this when it teaches from the Word of God. Therefore we do not believe unless we are taught from the Word of God, and this confirms our own position, and is the true sense of Augustine, who speaks there hypothetically, of unbelievers who are moved to believe by the authority of the Church, as in John 4: Many believed because of the woman's word, who afterwards said to the woman, Now we believe not because of your saying; for we have heard him ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world. For the weak, indeed, the authority of the Church seems greater, yet it is not in itself greater than the authority of the divine Word written. But we believe the Gospel, about which we have no doubt. The true Church, moreover, sets forth Scripture faithfully, and so the authority of the Church moves us. The ancient Fathers gave this reason: that the Church is founded on Scripture, and so they refuted all heretics from the Scriptures. What distinguishes the Nicene Council from the Council of Ariminum, if not Scripture? Thus those pious Fathers, in lawful councils, set forth Scripture against the heretics, as they had persevered in the doctrine of the Apostles; nor did they oppose to them the bare name of the Church. The heretics were refuted, and today they are to be refuted in the same way, because they profess a doctrine unknown and therefore contrary to holy Scripture.

units.la: D. j.
units.tr: D. j.

units.la: Cap.9.10.11. Arturus affirmat, Verbu Deiscri ptum etiamsi esset Ecclesiæ nota: tamen ad Luthe ranos & Caluinianos, quos vocat, non pertinere. Et cap.12. ad Rom. Ecclesiam, inquit, Verbum Dei spectat. Nonne Lutheri Ecclesia quæ vix se xagenaria: & Caluini quæ multo est iunior Trini tariorum quæ iam primum nascitur verbum Dei à Catholicis accepit: nonne Ecclesia Rom. integrum verbum Dei tutata est? non enim possunt dicere hæretici se mutilum aut mancum illud ab Ecclesia Rom. accepisse. At Caluiniani & Lutherani ver bum Dei interpretationibus suis depravant; illud verbu Dei corruperut versionibus, & aliis modis: Et lib.3.cap. 22. Vnde nobis Apostolica scripta, nisi ab Ecclesia Romana vere Apostolica? Et ta men aduersus eam profertis scripta Apostolica. Ingrati, perfidi. Abutuntur iis Veteres hæreses ex Scripturis astruunt de Iustif. fidei, &c. At Rom. Ecclesia illud accepit ab Apostolis, vt dicat cum Tertull. Mea est possessio: illa custodiut libros, non admisit omnes ad illorum lectionem, ne margaritas ante porcos proici ere videretur. Hæretici denique Rom. Ecclesiæ testimonio Scripturam esse Canoni cam didicerunt. Hæc ibi Arturus, Quum data opera agetur de fidei dogmatis, tum apparebit: rectene adhibeamus Scripturæ locos. Sed non sunt tractationes distinctæ confundendæ, vt Sophistæ facitant. Tota iltius argumenta tio vt vera esset, oporteret has demum propositiones esse veras & necessarias.
units.tr: At chapters 9, 10 and 11 Arturus asserts: Even if the written Word of God were known to the Church, yet it does not pertain to the Lutherans and Calvinists, as he calls them. And at chapter 12, on Romans: The Word of God, he says, looks to the Church. Is not the Lutheran church, which is scarcely sixty years old, and the Calvinist, which is much younger, and the Trinitarians, which is only now being born, did they not receive the Word of God from the Catholics? Has not the Roman Church preserved the whole Word of God? For heretics cannot say that they received it from the Roman Church mutilated or maimed. But the Calvinists and Lutherans corrupt the Word of God by their interpretations, and they have corrupted it by translations and in other ways. And in book 3, chapter 22: Whence do we have the apostolic writings, unless from the Roman Church, which is truly apostolic? And yet you set forth apostolic writings against her. Ungrateful, faithless men! The ancient heresies abuse them, and they assert from Scripture the doctrine of justification by faith, and so on. But the Roman Church received it from the Apostles, so that she may say with Tertullian, "It is my possession." She keeps the books, and has not admitted everyone to reading them, lest she seem to throw pearls before swine. Finally, the heretics learned from the testimony of the Roman Church that Scripture is canonical. So far Arturus. When the matter of the articles of faith is treated on purpose, it will then appear whether we use the passages of Scripture rightly. But distinct treatments should not be confused, as the Sophists do. The whole of his argument, to be true, would require that these propositions be true and necessary.

units.la: 1. Primum necessarium esset: Omnes qui sunt custodes S.Scripturæ esse veram Ecclesiā. At hæc propositio tanto abest vt sit necessaria, vt nec perpetuò vera sit. Non est necessaria: quia custodire libros S. Scripturæ, nó est causa cur sit Ecclesia : sed obseruare & retinere doctrinam quæ in illis libris sacris continetur. Quid enim est habere libros nisi instituta quæ in iis extant obserues? nec possumus definire Ecclesiam, nisi per id: quòd illa seruat legem Dei & doctrinam Euangelicam retineat, comprehensam in scriptis Propheticis & Apostolicis. Iuxta illud Non qui audiunt, sed qui seruant mandata Christi, sunt ipsius discipuli. Nec etiá est perpetuo vera illa Arturi propositio. Nam instantia labefactatur allatâ de Iudæis, quæ ges fuit custos & scriniaria Christianorum, bainlans legé & prophetas: vt loquitur Augustinus, qui hoc etiá addit, quod de Pontificiis merito possumus dicere. Iudæi, inquit, in libris suffragatores, in cordibus hostes, in codicibus testes. Agamus Deo gratias quòd non permiserit sanctos libros offusis pontificiis tenebris interire, quorum maximam partem extinctam velint. Sed age: habemus vetus Testamentum ab Ecclesia Israelitica in Synagogam, vt loquuntur veteres, degenerauit: iis exceptis qui Christum amplexi sunt. At enim Synagoga Iudaica libros sanctos etiamnum retinuit. Dicemúf-ne isthanc Synagogam idcirco veram Dei Ecclesiam esse: aut illos verbum Dei retinuisse? Sic hodie respondendum est Pontificiis dictitantibus se seruasse libros Canonicos à quorum tamen præscriptis discesserunt: & plurimas veteres hæreses, imò & vetustam Ethnicorum idolomaniam, nominibus tantum mutatis, retinuerunt. Sic Hierosolymis erat olim liber legis: & nihilominus Baal & Idola publice colebantur: & templum ipsum erat pollutum. 2. Reg. 22. 23. Pontificia Ecclesia thesaurum illum ita seruabat: nempe in tenebras S. Scripturam abdiderat, vt nemini propè pateret: pauci Doctores Romanenses, paucissimi Sacrificuli, vel ipsum nomen noui Testamenti tenebant. Plebs Paulum, Petrum & reliquos Apostolos, non aliter cognoscebat quam ex eorum statuis & picturis in templo collocatis, adeo vt quidam Papa Imagines vocaret libros idiotarum. Nam imaginibus Pastores Ecclesiae docendi curam demandarant. Erant-ne omnes Porci, quibus impurus iste dicit Ecclesiam Romanam noluisse margaritas proiicere? Quid? nonne tenetur quisque legem Dei noctes & dies meditari? Num conciones Christi & Apostolorum scripta ad paucissimos tantum pertinebant? Qua de re supra Chrysostomum loquentem audiimus. Nec propterea sunt omnes Doctores. Nam plebs Christiana legit Scripturam, vt melius doceatur.
units.tr: 1. First, it would have to be necessary that all who are guardians of Holy Scripture are the true Church. But this proposition is so far from being necessary that it is not even always true. It is not necessary, because keeping the books of Holy Scripture is not what makes a Church; rather, it is observing and retaining the doctrine contained in those holy books. For what is it to have books, unless you observe the precepts that are in them? Nor can we define the Church except by this: that she keeps the law of God and retains the evangelical doctrine comprehended in the prophetic and apostolic writings, according to the saying, It is not those who hear, but those who keep the commands of Christ, who are his disciples. Nor is Arturus's proposition always true. For the instance of the Jews refutes it, who were the guardians and keepers of the books of the Christians, bearing the law and the prophets, as Augustine says, and he adds what we may rightly say of the Papists: The Jews, he says, are supporters in the books, enemies in their hearts, witnesses in the codices. Let us thank God that he has not allowed the holy books to perish with the Papal darkness poured over them, most of which they would have extinguished. But come: we have the Old Testament, which the Israelite Church, as the ancients put it, degenerated into a synagogue, except for those who embraced Christ. Yet the Jewish synagogue has still retained the holy books. Shall we say, therefore, that this synagogue is for that reason the true Church of God, or that it has retained the Word of God? So today we must answer the Papists, who keep repeating that they have kept the canonical books, although they have departed from their prescriptions, and have retained many ancient heresies, and indeed the ancient idolatry of the heathen, with only the names changed. Thus at Jerusalem there was once the book of the law, and nevertheless Baal and idols were publicly worshipped, and the temple itself was polluted (2 Kings 22–23). The Papal Church kept that treasure in such a way: indeed it had hidden Holy Scripture in darkness, so that it was almost open to no one; few Roman teachers, very few sacrificing priests, even knew the very name of the New Testament. The common people knew Paul, Peter and the other apostles no otherwise than from their statues and pictures placed in the temple, so that a certain Pope called images the books of the unlearned. For they had entrusted the duty of teaching the people to images rather than to ministers of the Church. Were all of them swine, to whom this filthy man says the Roman Church was unwilling to throw pearls? What? Is not every person bound to meditate on the law of God day and night? Did the sermons of Christ and the writings of the Apostles pertain only to a very few? Concerning this we have heard Chrysostom speaking above. Nor, for that reason, are all of them teachers. For the Christian people reads Scripture so that it may be better taught.

units.la: Secundo vt Arturi argumenta haberent locum statuendae esset altera haec propositio, Rom. Ecclesiam S. Scripturae auctoritatem tribuere: quae oratio non modo falsa est, sed etiam blasphema & impia. Non igitur hic tantum agitur de solis libris custodiendis: sed de eorum veritudine quam nebulones impuri volunt Scripturae conciliari ex Pontificiae Romanae Ecclesiae auctoritate, quae nuper in Tridentina synodo libros Apocryphos cum Canoninonicis contrà veterum testimonia confudit. Arturus autem hic contrà se citauit August. lib. 32.cont. Faust. c.19. de Manichaeo loquens qui non auctoritati Scripturarum volebat subiici, sed ipse Scripturas sibi subiicere.
units.tr: Secondly, for Arturus's arguments to have any force, this other proposition would have to be established: that the Roman Church grants authority to Holy Scripture. This statement is not only false but also blasphemous and impious. Therefore the matter here is not merely the keeping of the books; it concerns their truth, which those impure rascals want to be established by the authority of the Papal Roman Church, which recently in the Tridentine synod confused the Apocryphal books with the canonical ones, against the testimony of the ancients. Arturus, moreover, here cites against himself Augustine, book 32 against Faustus, chapter 19, speaking of the Manichaean, who did not want to be subject to the authority of the Scriptures, but wanted to subject the Scriptures to himself.

units.la: Denique vt Arturus efficeret id quod vult, oporteret ipsum hanc propositionem probare: Ecclesiam Protestantium h. e. eorum qui Reformatam Religionem profitentur incepisse à Luthero. Nam hic ille petitione principij iitis Monachis consueta vtitur: qui nos etiam cum Anabaptistis & Antitrinitariis impudenter commiscent. Sed quod sine ratione affirmatur, sola negatione refellitur. Nihil enim hic audimus ex Arturo & reliquis Monachis eiusmodi praeter calumnias. Maiores pij Veteres ex verbo Dei refutarunt haereticos, atque ita docuerunt: Verbum Domini esse Notam Ecclesiae certissimam. Nos itidem vrgemus: & Patres admittimus vt admitti voluerunt: nempe quatenus cum verbo Dei & fidei analogiae congruunt. Et hanc partem concludimus ipsis Tertulliani verbis ab Arturo contra Arturum ad finem huius capitis producitis. Ego sum haeres Apostolorum, sicut cauerunt testamento suo, sicut fidei commiserunt, sicut adiurauerunt, ita teneo. Et audimus ibi Tertull. de praescr. haeret. Traditiones (quibus nituntur Pontificij) flagellantem. Ceterum vel ex Arturi verbis perspicuum est Verbum Dei scriptum esse Notam Ecclesiae certissimam. Nam quum vult nostras Ecclesias refellere, profert Scriptura, quamuis non aptè. Nos vero ex Scriptura ipsius argumentatione vere refutamus: vt probemus doctrinam Ecclesiæ Reformatæ ex S.Scriptura depromptam esse.
units.tr: Finally, for Arturus to achieve what he wants, he would have to prove this proposition himself: that the Protestant Church, that is, of those who profess the Reformed religion, began with Luther. For here he uses that petitio principii customary with the monks, who also shamelessly mix us up with the Anabaptists and Antitrinitarians. But what is affirmed without reason is refuted by denial alone. For we hear nothing from Arturus and the other monks of this kind except calumnies. The pious ancients refuted heretics from the Word of God, and so taught: that the Word of the Lord is the most certain mark of the Church. We likewise press this, and we admit the Fathers, as they wished to be admitted: namely, insofar as they agree with the Word of God and the analogy of faith. And we conclude this part with the very words of Tertullian, which Arturus, against Arturus, has brought forward at the end of this chapter: I am the heir of the Apostles; as they bound themselves by their testament, as they entrusted to the faith, as they adjured, so I hold. And there we hear Tertullian, in the Prescription against Heretics, scourging the traditions on which the Papists rely. Moreover, it is evident even from Arturus's own words that the written Word of God is the most certain mark of the Church. For when he wants to refute our churches, he brings forward Scripture, although not aptly. But we, from Scripture itself, refute him truly by its own argument, so as to prove that the doctrine of the Reformed Church is drawn from Holy Scripture.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: Chapter 6

units.la: ARturus libro tertio Notas Ecclesiæ ita tractat, vt modo quatuor, modo septem proponat. De Notis autem Ecclesiæ accurata fuit tractatio instituta in super. Analysi quam Arturus suis responsionibus nullo modo labefactat: item copiose de iis in Tract. de legitima vocat. pastorum: item aduersus Turrian. in Indice Artic. 8. 9. 15. 18. Et ad eiusdem sophismata loco Script. 1. Art. 22. & 30. Et adu. monachos Burdegal. Art. 60. 61. 62. 63. 51. Itaque hic erimus breviores, quum nihil afferat Arturus quod ibi non fuerit iam refutatum. Cæterum quū concilium Constantinop. dicit Ecclesiam vnam Sanctam, Catholicam & Apostolicam, potius indicat Qualis quam Quænam sit Ecclesia: sed quum docendum est quænam sit vera Christi Ecclesia & quid eam efficiat: tunc sunt ea proferenda quæ ipsius essentiam constituunt: nec accidentibus adhærescendum.
units.tr: Arturus, in book three, treats the marks of the Church in such a way that he sometimes proposes four and sometimes seven. The treatment of the marks of the Church was set out carefully in the earlier Analysis, which Arturus does not in any way shake with his replies. Likewise, I have discussed them fully in the Tract on the lawful calling of ministers, and against Turrian in the Index, Articles 8, 9, 15 and 18. For Arturus's sophisms, see Article 1 of the Scripture passage, and Articles 22 and 30. Against the Burgundian monks, see Articles 60 to 63 and 51. So I shall be briefer here, since Arturus brings forward nothing that has not already been refuted there. Moreover, when the Council of Constantinople says the Church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic, it indicates what sort of Church it is rather than which Church it is. But when we must teach which is the true Church of Christ and what makes it so, then we must set forth the things that constitute its essence, and not cling to accidents.

units.la: Assertor igitur Arturus Claritatem primam esse Ecclesiæ notam dicit lib. 3. cap. 1. & sequ. cuius hoc est argumetum. Hæretici semper pauperitate gloriati sunt vt docet veteres, &c. At Ecclesia Christiana semper futura est conspicua vt iidem docent & Prophetæ prædixerunt. Ecclesia autem Protestantium nō est conspicua, sed Romana. Ergo Roma Romana Ecclesia nō Protestantium est vera Christi Ecclesia. Huc redeunt quæcunque sex capitibus profert Arturus, ad quæ præter illa quæ suprà citauimus, notādum est: istum perperam hæreticos proferre qui paucitate gloriabātur. Nam Sadeel proposuit multitudinem non hominum quorundam tātūm, sed etiam Rerumpub. Regnorum & prouinciarum Religionem Reformatam amplectentium. Imò ipse Arturus paulò post nostros comparat cum decem Israelis tribubus, quarum maior erat Claritas (vt ille loquitur) quàm tribus Iudæ. Incepte igitur nunc paucitatem nobis obiicit. Verumtamen absurda fuit illorum hæreticorum ratiocinatio. Pauci sunt: ergo boni. & æque inepta est pontificiorum argumentatio illa. Multi sunt: ergo boni. Nam paucitas & multitudo non efficiunt probitatem aut bonitatem: sed sunt Accidentia ἐκ τῆς σωτηρίας & ἐνδεχομένων. Externus Ecclesiæ status non est in perpetuo statu conspicuus, vt apparet ex prophetis in veteri testamento & in nouo 2. Thess. 2. 4. Luc. 18. Matt. 24. Apoc. 13. &c. Ex quibus colligendum est, Ecclesiam Christi veram nō dici ex Multitudine aut ex Paucitate: sed ex fide & sinceritate doctrinæ: & internum splendorem considerandum esse, quem Pontificij recusant: externū tantum quærentes. Sed ille Assertor perinde agit de Ecclesiæ Claritate, ac si Sadeel constituerēt Ecclesiam perpetuò delitescentem: aut quasi Notam Ecclesiæ constituerent Obscuritatem, latebras & paucitatem: quòd esset doctrinam illorum imitari qui claritatē & splendorem notam Ecclesiæ proponentes Accidentibus separabilibus & sensibus externis perspicuis adhærescunt. Quis obscuro erat externus Ecclesiæ splendor quum ipsa à Tyrannis opprimebatur? Piorum tamen multitudo quoties existit commendanda est, & magni facienda.
units.tr: The advocate Arturus, then, says in book 3, chapter 1 and following, that clarity is the first mark of the Church, and his argument runs as follows: Heretics have always boasted of their poverty, as the ancients teach, etc. But the Christian Church will always be conspicuous, as the same writers teach and the prophets foretold. The Church of the Protestants, however, is not conspicuous, but the Roman one is. Therefore the Roman Church, not the Protestant one, is the true Church of Christ. All that Arturus brings forward in his six chapters comes back to this, and to it, besides what I have cited above, the following must be noted: he wrongly charges the heretics with boasting of their fewness. For Sadeel pointed to a multitude, not of a few individuals only, but also of commonwealths, kingdoms and provinces that embrace the Reformed religion. Indeed Arturus himself, a little later, compares our people with the ten tribes of Israel, of which, as he puts it, the greater was the clarity than the tribe of Judah. So now he objects to us our fewness, having begun from a different point. Yet the reasoning of those heretics was absurd: they are few, therefore they are good. And that Papist argument is equally silly: they are many, therefore they are good. For fewness and multitude do not produce holiness or goodness; they are accidents [ἐκ τῆς σωτηρίας] and [ἐνδεχομένων]. The outward state of the Church is not always conspicuous, as appears from the prophets in the Old Testament and in the New from 2 Thess. 2, Luke 18, Matt. 24, Rev. 13, etc. From these passages it must be concluded that the true Church of Christ is not named from multitude or from paucity, but from faith and the purity of doctrine; and that its inner brightness must be considered, which the Papists refuse, seeking only the outward. But that advocate deals with the clarity of the Church as if Sadeel had set up a Church that always lies hidden, or as if they made obscurity, hiding places and fewness the mark of the Church. This would be to imitate those who, proposing clarity and splendour as the mark of the Church, cling to separable accidents and to outward perceptible signs. How obscure was the outward splendour of the Church when it was oppressed by tyrants? Yet the multitude of the godly, wherever it exists, is to be commended and held in high esteem.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: ASsertor iste libro 3. cap. 7.8. 9. & 10. impugnat septimum caput Analysis superioris vt Diffusione per orbem terrarum Notam Ecclesiæ secundâ, câmq; ad Ecclesiam Rom. pertinere, ostendat. Atque hinc Romanam Ecclesiā esse veram Ecclesiam: Protestantium vero falsam colligit. Maiorem illam vt probet, promissiones de Ecclesiæ & doctrinæ Christianæ propagatione profert. Sed in Minori hæret. Nam calumniis duntaxat eam munit: & nusquam probat illa testimonia & promissiones ad Romanam Ecclesiam pertinere. Hinc fit vt Minor nihil commune habeat cum Maiore propositione: ac proinde Conclusio fit ex illis perperam instituta. Sed de hac Ecclesiæ nota aduersus Turrianum eadem quę Arturus proferentem, copiosè præsertim in Indice Art. 15. disputatum est. Hic igitur hæc Theoremata tanquam quædam Corollaria tantum proponimus: reliqua sunt ex copiosiore illa disputatione petenda.
units.tr: This author, in chapters 7, 8, 9 and 10 of his third book, attacks the seventh chapter of the earlier Analysis, where it is shown that diffusion throughout the world is the second mark of the Church and that this mark belongs to the Roman Church. From this he concludes that the Roman Church is the true Church and that the Protestant churches are false. To prove the major premise, he brings forward promises concerning the spread of the Church and of Christian doctrine. But he sticks on the minor premise. He defends it only with slanders, and nowhere proves that those testimonies and promises pertain to the Roman Church. Hence the minor premise has nothing in common with the major, and so the conclusion drawn from them is wrongly constructed. But this mark of the Church was already discussed at length against Turrianus, in the same way as Arturus put it forward, especially in the Index, article 15. Here, therefore, we offer these propositions only as corollaries; the rest is to be sought in that fuller discussion.

units.la: 1. Vera Ecclesia Christiana ad quam pertinet promissiones quæ extant in prophetis, vt Esa. 2.54. &c. diffusa fuit per Apostolorum prædi-catiónem cui nos adhærescimus, ac proinde nostra est Ecclesia: adeò vt illius Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ propagatio ad nostram Ecclesiā etiam pertineat. Nostram enim doctrinā, esse Apostolorum doctrinā demonstramus. Vnitas autem Ecclesiæ, est in doctrina, inquit Tertullianus. Ergo, Examinanda est doctrina: nec sunt spectanda quædam Accidentia quæ ad rei sententiam non spectant.
units.tr: 1. The true Christian Church, to which the promises found in the prophets pertain, as in Isaiah 54 and following, was spread through the preaching of the Apostles, to which we adhere; and therefore our church is that church. So much so that the spread of that Apostolic Church also pertains to our church. For we show that our doctrine is the doctrine of the Apostles. Moreover, the unity of the Church lies in doctrine, says Tertullian. Therefore doctrine must be examined, and we must not look at certain accidents that have no bearing on the substance of the matter.

units.la: 2. Etsi Diffusio quâ Pontificij vrgent non sit vera Ecclesiæ nota: eâ tamen habent Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, licet illam impedire conetur Monachorū collunies, flammis nequicquâ in nos accensis, gladiis & variis artibus excitatis.
units.tr: 2. Even if the diffusion on which the Papists insist is not a true mark of the Church, the Reformed churches nevertheless have it, although the conspiracies of the monks try to hinder it, with flames kindled against us to no avail, and with swords and various arts stirred up.

units.la: 3. Scriptura non promittit Ecclesiæ perpetuam amplitudinē. Hoc in Ecclesia Israëlitica ex Prophetis apparet. In Christiana verò, id experientia comprobat. Percurre Ecclesias Orientis & Africæ nunc desertas, olim splendidissimas. Illud si Oriēti contigit, cur non & potuit Occidenti?
units.tr: 3. Scripture does not promise the Church perpetual extent. This is evident in the Israelite Church from the Prophets. In the Christian Church, experience confirms it. Run through the churches of the East and of Africa, now deserted, once most splendid. If this has happened to the East, why could it not also happen to the West?

units.la: 4. Ecclesia prisca Apostolica vel Christiana ignorauit splendoré illū qui lucet in aula pōtificis, in purpura Cardinalium, Mitra Episcoporum & superstitione innumerabilium Monachorum.
units.tr: 4. The ancient Apostolic or Christian Church knew nothing of that splendour which shines in the papal court, in the purple of the Cardinals, the mitre of the Bishops, and the superstition of countless monks.

units.la: 5. Deus semper excitauit viros pios qui erroribus obsisterent: Sed quis miretur in tam crassis tenebris pios illos in multis fuisse hallucinatos? qui tamē fundamentū veræ doctrinæ retinebant: ac proinde verā Ecclesiā constituebant. Nec enim quilibet errores Ecclesiam perimunt: sicut nec quilibet morbi iugulant homines.
units.tr: 5. God has always raised up godly men who resisted errors. But who would be surprised that those godly men, in such thick darkness, were in many things led astray? Yet they retained the foundation of true doctrine, and therefore they constituted a true Church. For not every error destroys a Church, just as not every disease kills a man.

units.la: 6. Cótinuatio doctrinæ potest esse absque illa Diffusione & Amplitudine. An negabis cundé esse fluuium nisi perpetuò exúdet? Diffusio autem & Amplitudo nó potest esse vera Ecclesiæ nota propria, Reciproca & Adæquata, quia etiam impiis cœtibus, vt Turcis, Ethnicis, Iudæis conuenit.
units.tr: 6. Continuance of doctrine can exist without that diffusion and extent. Will you deny that a river is a river unless it always overflows? Yet diffusion and extent cannot be a proper, reciprocal and adequate mark of the true Church, because they also belong to impious assemblies, such as the Turks, the heathens and the Jews.

units.la: 7. Exoriente Euangelij sole ingentes hæreticorum nubes & tetræ exhalationes illam lucé obscurare conátur: Conatur Sata tenebras luci veritatis effundere, ideò impuros, impios, & Ecclesiarum varios perturbatores excitat. Hoc in Ecclesia prisca cóprobatur: hoc etiam renascente Ecclesia experimur: Hæreticis variis illas perturbantibus: qui suas hæreses ex tenebris pontificiis maximè hauriunt: vt olim in Ecclesia prisca, ex Ethnicis & Iudæis sua portenta hæretici & Mahumetani deprompserút.
units.tr: 7. When the sun of the Gospel rises, huge clouds of heretics and foul exhalations try to darken that light. Satan tries to pour darkness over the light of truth, and therefore he stirs up impure and impious men and various disturbers of the churches. This is proved in the ancient Church; we also experience it as the Church is reborn, with various heretics disturbing it, who very largely draw their heresies from Papist darkness, just as in the ancient Church heretics and Mahometans drew their monstrosities from the heathens and the Jews.

units.la: Ex his paucis lectores satis iudicabunt quid de Arturi argumentis & calumniis sit statuendū. Ex his etiá futile & nugatoriū esse argumētū istius euincitur, quod tamé ab ipso vocatur. Graue atque solidum & quod μὴ ἐνδίχεται λύειν: Ecclesia, inquit, vera diffundi per omnes gentes debet. Vetera nec diffusa fuit olim, nec in præsentia, nec unquam diffundetur. Non est ergo vera Ecclesia. Maior propositio sic statuēda. Veram nimirum Ecclesiā Christianā nullis vel gentiū vel locorū terminis circunscribi: quæ diffusa fuit Apostolorū tepore: sed non semper in eodē statu manet, nec semper vbique diffunditur. Minor propositio euertitur ex eo quod doceamus eã ipsam, esse illã Christiana & Apostolicam, quæ etiam his temporibus Dei beneficio longè latéque propagatur.
units.tr: From these few points the readers will judge sufficiently what is to be decided about Arturus's arguments and slanders. From these points it is also shown that the argument of this man, though it is called his own, is futile and trifling. It is weighty and solid in the sense that it cannot be refuted [μὴ ἐνδίχεται λύειν]: The true Church, he says, must be spread through all nations. The ancient Church was not spread then, nor is it now, nor will it ever be spread. Therefore it is not the true Church. The major premise should be stated thus: the true Christian Church is bounded by no limits of nations or places, and it was spread in the time of the Apostles, but it does not always remain in the same state, nor is it always spread everywhere. The minor premise is overturned by the fact that we teach that this very church is the Christian and Apostolic Church, which even in these times, by God's blessing, is propagated far and wide.

units.la: Porrò Diffusio illa nullã cōtinet causã quare Ecclesia sit vera: imò est cōmune & vagū accidens: Ergo Syllogismus ille nō confectus est ex necessario Mediotac proinde non est <bl>ἀπόδ</bl>ειξις nec Apodeicticus. Est deniq; ἆθεόλογος quia nullo nititur Axiomate ex sacra Scriptura deprompto, εὔλυτος etiam est, quòd Minor eius propositio ἀγνοίαν ἐλέγχει & petitionem principij contineat.
units.tr: Moreover, that diffusion contains no cause why the Church should be true; indeed it is a common and wandering accident. Therefore that syllogism is not constructed from a necessary middle term, and so it is not a demonstration [ἀπόδειξις] nor demonstrative.
